title: Nuzhat al-alibbāʾ fī ṭabaqāt al-udabāʾ
printTitle: نُزْهَةُ الْأَلِبَّا فِي طَبَقَاتِ الْأُدَبَا، أَيِ النُّحَاةِ
author: Abū al-Barakāt ibn al-Anbārī
authorArabic: أَبُو الْبَرَكَاتِ كَمَالُ الدِّينِ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْأَنْبَارِيُّ

edition.title: Nuzhat al-alibbā fī ṭabaqāt al-udabā, ay al-nuḥāh
edition.copy: Cornell University Library, PJ 6063 .I2 1877 (Arabic Collections Online, cornell_aco000193)

introduction: Nuzhat al-alibbāʾ fī ṭabaqāt al-udabāʾ, 'The delight of the discerning: on the generations of the men of letters', is the history of the grammarians written by Abū al-Barakāt ibn al-Anbārī (d. 577/1181), who taught grammar at the Niẓāmiyya of Baghdad. Its entries follow one another in the order of their deaths, from Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, with whom the book opens by the story of ʿAlī's sheet, to the author's own teacher Ibn al-Shajarī (d. 542/1148); it closes with Ibn al-Anbārī's own chain of teachers back to ʿAlī.

By udabāʾ the book means the masters of the sciences of the Arabic language. Most of its men are the grammarians and lexicographers of Basra, Kufa and Baghdad, but the transmitters of the old poetry are there too, and the poets who were authorities on the language, such as Abū Nuwās, Abū Tammām, al-Mutanabbī and Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī. An entry gives a scholar's name, his teachers and pupils, his books, a few reports about him (a debate, a mistake caught, a line of verse) and, where it is known, the year he died. Most entries are short: where the older books gave long chains of narrators, Ibn al-Anbārī usually names only the first, and much of what later writers such as Yāqūt tell of the grammarians passed through his book.

Here the book is the backbone of the scholars: every entry has a page of its own, with the Arabic as the print has it and our English under each paragraph, and is tied to the scholar's page where there is one. The list below sets the entries out by the century in which their men died, with the number each has in the book.

The text follows the first print, the Cairo lithograph of 1294/1877 (al-Maṭābiʿ al-Miṣriyya), whose title page reads Nuzhat al-alibbā fī ṭabaqāt al-udabā, ay al-nuḥāh, 'that is, the grammarians'; the scan is of the copy in Cornell University Library, in Arabic Collections Online. The page numbers are the print's. The print has few vowels, so the vocalisation is ours; doubtful readings are noted. The modern editions are not used.

preface.ar: بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ خَالِقِ الْإِنْسَانِ، الَّذِي عَلَّمَهُ الْبَيَانَ، وَالصَّلَاةُ الدَّائِمَةُ عَلَى سَيِّدِنَا مُحَمَّدٍ نَبِيِّهِ وَصَفْوَتِهِ مِنَ الْأَكْوَانِ، وَعَلَى آلِهِ وَصَحْبِهِ مَا أَبَنَّ أَبَانٌ، وَأَعْرَبَ لِسَانٌ وَأَبَانَ.
preface.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, the Creator of man, who taught him clear speech; and lasting blessing upon our master Muḥammad, His Prophet and His chosen one among all beings, and upon his family and his Companions, as long as Mount Abān stands firm and a tongue speaks correctly and makes its meaning plain.

preface.ar: وَبَعْدُ، فَقَدْ ذَكَرْتُ فِي هٰذَا الْكِتَابِ الْمَوْسُومِ بِنُزْهَةِ الْأَلِبَّا فِي طَبَقَاتِ الْأُدَبَا مَعَارِفَ أَهْلِ هٰذِهِ الصِّنَاعَةِ الْأَعْيَانِ، وَمَنْ قَارَبَهُمْ فِي الْفَضْلِ وَالْإِتْقَانِ، وَبَيَّنْتُ أَحْوَالَهُمْ وَأَزْمَانَهُمْ عَلَى غَايَةٍ مِنَ الْكَشْفِ وَالْبَيَانِ، فَاللهُ تَعَالَى يَمُنُّ بِهِ، إِنَّهُ الْكَرِيمُ الْمَنَّانُ.
preface.en: To proceed: in this book, entitled Nuzhat al-alibbāʾ fī ṭabaqāt al-udabāʾ (The Delight of the Discerning on the Generations of the Men of Letters), I have set down what is known of the eminent masters of this craft and of those who came close to them in excellence and mastery, and I have set out their lives and their times as clearly and plainly as can be. May God, exalted is He, grant His favour through it; He is the Generous, the Bestower of favours.

entries.heading: أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ
entries.name: Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī

paragraphs.ar:
اِعْلَمْ، أَيَّدَكَ اللهُ تَعَالَى بِالتَّوْفِيقِ، وَأَرْشَدَكَ إِلَى سَوَاءِ الطَّرِيقِ، أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ عِلْمَ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ، وَأَسَّسَ قَوَاعِدَهُ، وَحَدَّ حُدُودَهُ، أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ، وَأَخَذَ عَنْهُ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ، وَهُوَ مَنْسُوبٌ إِلَى الدُّئِلِ بْنِ بَكْرِ بْنِ كِنَانَةَ، وَالدُّئِلُ عَلَى فُعِلٍ اسْمُ دُوَيْبَّةٍ سُمِّيَ الرَّجُلُ بِهَا، قَالَ سِيبَوَيْهِ: وَلَيْسَ فِي لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ اسْمٌ عَلَى وَزْنِ فُعِلٍ غَيْرُهُ، وَأَنْشَدَ:
جَاؤُوا بِجَيْشٍ لَوْ قِيسَ مُعْرَسُهُ * مَا كَانَ إِلَّا كَمُعْرَسِ الدُّئِلِ
paragraphs.en: Know, may God, exalted is He, strengthen you with success and guide you to the right path, that the first to lay down the science of Arabic, to found its rules and to define its limits was the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him, and Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī took it from him. He is named after al-Duʾil ibn Bakr ibn Kināna; al-duʾil, on the pattern fuʿil, is the name of a small animal after which the man was named. Sībawayh said: there is no noun in the language of the Arabs on the pattern fuʿil besides it; and he recited: They came with an army whose camping ground, were it measured, would be no bigger than the camping ground of a duʾil.

paragraphs.ar: وَحَكَى غَيْرُهُ: رُئِمٌ اسْمٌ لِلِاسْتِ، وَوُعِلٌ فِي الْوَعِلِ، وَالدِّيلُ فِي عَبْدِ الْقَيْسِ، وَالدُّوَلُ فِي حَنِيفَةَ.
paragraphs.en: Others report also ruʾim, a name for the backside, and wuʿil for waʿil (the mountain goat); and they say that al-Dīl is a clan of ʿAbd al-Qays, and al-Duwal a clan of Ḥanīfa.

paragraphs.ar: وَسَبَبُ وَضْعِ عَلِيٍّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لِهٰذَا الْعِلْمِ
paragraphs.en: Why ʿAlī, peace be upon him, laid down this science

paragraphs.ar: مَا رَوَى أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ، قَالَ: دَخَلْتُ عَلَى أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ، فَوَجَدْتُ فِي يَدِهِ رُقْعَةً، فَقُلْتُ: مَا هٰذِهِ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ؟ فَقَالَ: إِنِّي تَأَمَّلْتُ كَلَامَ الْعَرَبِ فَوَجَدْتُهُ قَدْ فَسَدَ بِمُخَالَطَةِ هٰذِهِ الْحَمْرَاءِ، يَعْنِي الْأَعَاجِمَ، فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَضَعَ شَيْئًا يَرْجِعُونَ إِلَيْهِ، وَيَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَيْهِ. ثُمَّ أَلْقَى إِلَيَّ الرُّقْعَةَ، وَفِيهَا مَكْتُوبٌ: الْكَلَامُ كُلُّهُ اسْمٌ وَفِعْلٌ وَحَرْفٌ؛ فَالِاسْمُ مَا أَنْبَأَ عَنِ الْمُسَمَّى، وَالْفِعْلُ مَا أُنْبِئَ بِهِ، وَالْحَرْفُ مَا أَفَادَ مَعْنًى. وَقَالَ لِي: اُنْحُ هٰذَا النَّحْوَ، وَأَضِفْ إِلَيْهِ مَا وَقَعَ إِلَيْكَ، وَاعْلَمْ يَا أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ أَنَّ الْأَسْمَاءَ ثَلَاثَةٌ: ظَاهِرٌ، وَمُضْمَرٌ، وَاسْمٌ لَا ظَاهِرٌ وَلَا مُضْمَرٌ، وَإِنَّمَا يَتَفَاضَلُ النَّاسُ يَا أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ فِيمَا لَيْسَ بِظَاهِرٍ وَلَا مُضْمَرٍ، وَأَرَادَ بِذٰلِكَ الِاسْمَ الْمُبْهَمَ.
paragraphs.en: It is what Abū al-Aswad related. He said: I went in to the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him, and found a slip of paper in his hand. I said: What is this, Commander of the Faithful? He said: I have considered the speech of the Arabs and found that it has become corrupted through mixing with these red-faced people, meaning the non-Arabs, so I wanted to lay down something to which they can return and on which they can rely. Then he tossed the slip to me, and on it was written: Speech is all noun, verb and particle. The noun is what tells of the thing named; the verb is what is told of it; and the particle is what conveys a meaning. And he said to me: Follow this course (unḥu hādhā al-naḥw), and add to it whatever comes your way. And know, Abū al-Aswad, that nouns are three: the overt, the concealed, and a noun that is neither overt nor concealed; and people excel one another, Abū al-Aswad, only in what is neither overt nor concealed. By this he meant the vague noun (al-ism al-mubham).

paragraphs.ar: قَالَ: ثُمَّ وَضَعْتُ بَابَيِ الْعَطْفِ وَالنَّعْتِ، ثُمَّ بَابَيِ التَّعَجُّبِ وَالِاسْتِفْهَامِ، إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلْتُ إِلَى بَابِ إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، مَا خَلَا لٰكِنَّ، فَلَمَّا عَرَضْتُهَا عَلَى عَلِيٍّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ أَمَرَنِي بِضَمِّ لٰكِنَّ إِلَيْهَا، وَكُنْتُ كُلَّمَا وَضَعْتُ بَابًا مِنْ أَبْوَابِ النَّحْوِ عَرَضْتُهُ عَلَيْهِ رَضِيَ اللهُ تَعَالَى عَنْهُ، إِلَى أَنْ حَصَّلْتُ مَا فِيهِ الْكِفَايَةُ، قَالَ: مَا أَحْسَنَ هٰذَا النَّحْوَ الَّذِي قَدْ نَحَوْتَ! فَلِذٰلِكَ سُمِّيَ النَّحْوَ.
paragraphs.en: He said: Then I laid down the two chapters of the conjunction and the qualifier, then the two chapters of wonder and the question, until I reached the chapter of inna and its sisters, leaving out lākinna. When I showed them to ʿAlī, peace be upon him, he told me to add lākinna to them. Every time I laid down a chapter of grammar I showed it to him, God be pleased with him, until I had gathered what was sufficient. He said: How fine is this course (naḥw) that you have followed! For that reason it was called naḥw.

paragraphs.ar:
وَكَانَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ مِمَّنْ صَحِبَ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَلِيَّ بْنَ أَبِي طَالِبٍ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ، وَكَانَ مِنَ الْمَشْهُورِينَ بِصُحْبَتِهِ وَمَحَبَّتِهِ وَمَحَبَّةِ أَهْلِ بَيْتِهِ، وَفِي ذٰلِكَ يَقُولُ:
يَقُولُ الْأَرْذَلُونَ بَنُو قُشَيْرٍ * طَوَالَ الدَّهْرِ لَا تَنْسَى عَلِيَّا
فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ تَرْكِي * مِنَ الْأَشْيَاءِ مَا يُحْصَى عَلَيَّا
أُحِبُّ مُحَمَّدًا حُبًّا شَدِيدًا * وَعَبَّاسًا وَحَمْزَةَ وَالْوَصِيَّا
فَإِنْ يَكُ حُبُّهُمْ رُشْدًا أُصِبْهُ * وَفِيهِمْ أُسْوَةٌ إِنْ كَانَ غَيَّا
فَكَمْ رُشْدًا أَصَبْتُ وَحُزْتُ مَجْدًا * تَقَاصَرُ دُونَهُ هَامُ الثُّرَيَّا
paragraphs.en: Abū al-Aswad was one of those who kept company with the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, peace be upon him, and he was well known for his companionship with him and his love of him and of the people of his house. On this he says: The basest of men, the Banū Qushayr, say: For all time you will not forget ʿAlī. I said to them: How could I give up, of all things, what will be reckoned to my account? I love Muḥammad with a strong love, and ʿAbbās and Ḥamza and the Testamentary Heir. If loving them is right guidance, I shall attain it; and if it is error, there is a good example in them. How much right guidance have I attained, and how much glory have I won, beneath which the heads of the Pleiades fall short!

paragraphs.ar: وَكَانَ يَنْزِلُ الْبَصْرَةَ فِي بَنِي قُشَيْرٍ، وَكَانُوا يَرْجُمُونَهُ بِاللَّيْلِ لِمَحَبَّتِهِ عَلِيًّا وَأَهْلَ بَيْتِهِ، فَإِذَا ذَكَرَ رَجْمَهُمْ لَهُ قَالُوا: إِنَّ اللهَ تَعَالَى يَرْجُمُكَ، فَيَقُولُ لَهُمْ: تَكْذِبُونَ، لَوْ رَجَمَنِي اللهُ أَصَابَنِي، وَلٰكِنَّكُمْ تَرْجُمُونَ فَلَا تُصِيبُونَ.
paragraphs.en: He lived in Basra among the Banū Qushayr, and they used to stone him at night for his love of ʿAlī and the people of his house. When he spoke of their stoning him, they would say: It is God, exalted is He, who stones you. He would say to them: You lie. If God stoned me, He would hit me; but you stone and do not hit.

paragraphs.ar: وَرُوِيَ أَنَّ سَبَبَ وَضْعِ عَلِيٍّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لِهٰذَا الْعِلْمِ أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ أَعْرَابِيًّا يَقْرَأُ: «لَا يَأْكُلُهُ إِلَّا الْخَاطِئِينَ»، فَوَضَعَ النَّحْوَ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that the reason ʿAlī, peace be upon him, laid down this science was that he heard a Bedouin recite: “None eat it but the sinners (al-khāṭiʾīna)”, in the accusative; so he laid down grammar.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُرْوَى أَيْضًا أَنَّهُ قَدِمَ أَعْرَابِيٌّ فِي خِلَافَةِ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ، فَقَالَ: مَنْ يُقْرِئُنِي شَيْئًا مِمَّا أَنْزَلَ اللهُ تَعَالَى عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ؟ فَأَقْرَأَهُ رَجُلٌ سُورَةَ بَرَاءَةَ، فَقَالَ: «أَنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولِهِ» بِالْجَرِّ، فَقَالَ الْأَعْرَابِيُّ: أَوَقَدْ بَرِئَ اللهُ مِنْ رَسُولِهِ؟ إِنْ يَكُنِ اللهُ تَعَالَى بَرِئَ مِنْ رَسُولِهِ فَأَنَا أَبْرَأُ مِنْهُ. فَبَلَغَ عُمَرَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ مَقَالَةُ الْأَعْرَابِيِّ، فَدَعَاهُ فَقَالَ: يَا أَعْرَابِيُّ، أَتَبْرَأُ مِنْ رَسُولِ اللهِ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ؟ فَقَالَ: يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، إِنِّي قَدِمْتُ الْمَدِينَةَ وَلَا عِلْمَ لِي بِالْقُرْآنِ، فَسَأَلْتُ مَنْ يُقْرِئُنِي، فَأَقْرَأَنِي هٰذَا سُورَةَ بَرَاءَةَ، فَقَالَ: «أَنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولِهِ»، فَقُلْتُ: أَوَقَدْ بَرِئَ اللهُ تَعَالَى مِنْ رَسُولِهِ؟ إِنْ يَكُنِ اللهُ تَعَالَى بَرِئَ مِنْ رَسُولِهِ فَأَنَا أَبْرَأُ مِنْهُ. فَقَالَ عُمَرُ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ: لَيْسَ هٰكَذَا يَا أَعْرَابِيُّ. فَقَالَ: كَيْفَ هِيَ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ؟ فَقَالَ: «أَنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولُهُ». فَقَالَ الْأَعْرَابِيُّ: وَأَنَا وَاللهِ أَبْرَأُ مِمَّنْ بَرِئَ اللهُ وَرَسُولُهُ مِنْهُمْ. فَأَمَرَ عُمَرُ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ أَنْ لَا يُقْرِئَ الْقُرْآنَ إِلَّا عَالِمٌ بِاللُّغَةِ، وَأَمَرَ أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيَّ أَنْ يَضَعَ النَّحْوَ.
paragraphs.en: It is also related that a Bedouin came during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, God be pleased with him, and said: Who will teach me to recite something of what God, exalted is He, sent down to Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace? A man taught him to recite Sūrat Barāʾa, and recited: “that God is quit of the idolaters, and of His Messenger” (wa-rasūlihi), in the genitive. The Bedouin said: Has God then become quit of His Messenger? If God, exalted is He, has become quit of His Messenger, then I am quit of him. The Bedouin's words reached ʿUmar, peace be upon him, and he summoned him and said: Bedouin, do you declare yourself quit of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace? He said: Commander of the Faithful, I came to Medina with no knowledge of the Qurʾān, and I asked who would teach me to recite; this man taught me Sūrat Barāʾa and recited: “that God is quit of the idolaters, and of His Messenger.” I said: Has God, exalted is He, then become quit of His Messenger? If God, exalted is He, has become quit of His Messenger, then I am quit of him. ʿUmar, God be pleased with him, said: It is not so, Bedouin. He said: How is it, Commander of the Faithful? He said: “that God is quit of the idolaters, and so is His Messenger” (wa-rasūluhu). The Bedouin said: And I, by God, am quit of those of whom God and His Messenger are quit. ʿUmar, God be pleased with him, then ordered that none but one learned in the language should teach the Qurʾān, and he ordered Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī to lay down grammar.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ مَعْمَرُ بْنُ الْمُثَنَّى وَغَيْرُهُ: أَخَذَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ النَّحْوَ عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ.
paragraphs.en: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā and others said: Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī took grammar from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, God be pleased with him.

paragraphs.ar: وَرُوِيَ أَيْضًا أَنَّ زِيَادَ ابْنَ أَبِيهِ بَعَثَ إِلَى أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيِّ وَقَالَ لَهُ: يَا أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ، إِنَّ هٰذِهِ الْحَمْرَاءَ قَدْ كَثُرَتْ، وَأَفْسَدَتْ مِنْ أَلْسُنِ الْعَرَبِ، فَلَوْ وَضَعْتَ لَهُمْ شَيْئًا يُقِيمُونَ بِهِ كَلَامَهُمْ! فَأَبَى عَلَيْهِ. فَبَعَثَ زِيَادٌ رَجُلًا وَقَالَ لَهُ: اُقْعُدْ عَلَى طَرِيقِ أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، فَإِذَا مَرَّ بِكَ فَاقْرَأْ شَيْئًا مِنَ الْقُرْآنِ، وَتَعَمَّدِ اللَّحْنَ فِيهِ. فَقَعَدَ ذٰلِكَ الرَّجُلُ عَلَى طَرِيقِ أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، فَلَمَّا مَرَّ بِهِ رَفَعَ صَوْتَهُ وَقَرَأَ: «أَنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولِهِ»، فَاسْتَعْظَمَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ ذٰلِكَ وَقَالَ: عَزَّ وَجْهُ اللهِ تَعَالَى أَنْ يَبْرَأَ مِنْ رَسُولِهِ! وَرَجَعَ مِنْ فَوْرِهِ إِلَى زِيَادٍ فَقَالَ: يَا هٰذَا، قَدْ أَجَبْتُكَ إِلَى مَا سَأَلْتَ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَنْ أَبْدَأَ بِإِعْرَابِ الْقُرْآنِ، فَابْعَثْ إِلَيَّ ثَلَاثِينَ رَجُلًا. فَأَحْضَرَهُمْ زِيَادٌ، فَاخْتَارَ مِنْهُمْ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ عَشَرَةً، ثُمَّ لَمْ يَزَلْ يَخْتَارُهُمْ حَتَّى اخْتَارَ مِنْهُمْ رَجُلًا مِنْ عَبْدِ الْقَيْسِ، فَقَالَ: خُذِ الْمُصْحَفَ وَصِبْغًا يُخَالِفُ لَوْنَ الْمِدَادِ، فَإِذَا فَتَحْتُ شَفَتَيَّ فَانْقُطْ وَاحِدَةً فَوْقَ الْحَرْفِ، وَإِذَا ضَمَمْتُهُمَا فَاجْعَلِ النُّقْطَةَ إِلَى جَانِبِ الْحَرْفِ، وَإِذَا كَسَرْتُهُمَا فَاجْعَلِ النُّقْطَةَ فِي أَسْفَلِهِ، فَإِنْ أَتْبَعْتُ شَيْئًا مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْحَرَكَاتِ غُنَّةً فَانْقُطْ نُقْطَتَيْنِ. فَابْتَدَأَ بِالْمُصْحَفِ حَتَّى أَتَى عَلَى آخِرِهِ، ثُمَّ وَضَعَ الْمُخْتَصَرَ الْمَنْسُوبَ إِلَيْهِ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ.
paragraphs.en: It is also related that Ziyād ibn Abīhi sent for Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī and said to him: Abū al-Aswad, these red-faced people have grown many and have corrupted the tongues of the Arabs; if only you would lay down something for them by which they could set their speech right! He refused him. So Ziyād sent a man and said to him: Sit on Abū al-Aswad's road, and when he passes you, recite something of the Qurʾān and make a mistake in it on purpose. The man sat on Abū al-Aswad's road, and when he passed by he raised his voice and recited: “that God is quit of the idolaters, and of His Messenger.” Abū al-Aswad found that monstrous and said: Exalted is the face of God, exalted is He, above being quit of His Messenger! He went straight back to Ziyād and said: Sir, I grant you what you asked. I think I should begin with the declension (iʿrāb) of the Qurʾān; send me thirty men. Ziyād brought them, and Abū al-Aswad chose ten of them; then he went on choosing among them until he chose one man of ʿAbd al-Qays, and said: Take the copy of the Qurʾān and a dye of another colour than the ink. When I open my lips, put one dot above the letter; when I bring them together, put the dot beside the letter; when I part them downwards, put the dot beneath it; and if I let one of these vowels be followed by a nasal sound, put two dots. So he began the copy and went through it to its end. After that he composed the abridgement that is ascribed to him.

paragraphs.ar: وَرَوَى عَاصِمٌ قَالَ: جَاءَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ إِلَى زِيَادٍ، وَهُوَ أَمِيرُ الْبَصْرَةِ، فَقَالَ: إِنِّي أَرَى الْعَرَبَ قَدْ خَالَطَتْ هٰذِهِ الْأَعَاجِمَ، وَفَسَدَتْ أَلْسِنَتُهَا، أَفَتَأْذَنُ لِي أَنْ أَضَعَ لِلْعَرَبِ مَا يَعْرِفُونَ بِهِ كَلَامَهُمْ؟ فَقَالَ لَهُ زِيَادٌ: لَا تَفْعَلْ. قَالَ: فَجَاءَ رَجُلٌ إِلَى زِيَادٍ فَقَالَ: أَصْلَحَ اللهُ الْأَمِيرَ، تُوُفِّيَ أَبَانَا وَتَرَكَ بَنُونَا. فَقَالَ لَهُ زِيَادٌ: تُوُفِّيَ أَبَانَا وَتَرَكَ بَنُونَا! اُدْعُ لِي أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ. فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُ قَالَ لَهُ: ضَعْ لِلنَّاسِ مَا كُنْتُ نَهَيْتُكَ عَنْهُ. فَفَعَلَ.
paragraphs.en: ʿĀṣim related: Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī came to Ziyād, who was then governor of Basra, and said: I see that the Arabs have mixed with these non-Arabs and their tongues have become corrupted. Will you permit me to lay down for the Arabs something by which they may know their speech? Ziyād said to him: Do not. Then a man came to Ziyād and said: May God keep the governor in good health, “our father (abānā) has died and left sons (banūnā)”. Ziyād said to him: “Our father has died and left sons”! Call Abū al-Aswad to me. When he came, he said to him: Lay down for the people what I had forbidden you to. And he did.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُرْوَى عَنْهُ أَيْضًا أَنَّ أَبَا الْأَسْوَدِ قَالَتْ لَهُ ابْنَتُهُ: مَا أَحْسَنُ السَّمَاءِ! فَقَالَ لَهَا: نُجُومُهَا. فَقَالَتْ: إِنِّي لَمْ أُرِدْ هٰذَا، وَإِنَّمَا تَعَجَّبْتُ مِنْ حُسْنِهَا. فَقَالَ لَهَا: إِذَنْ فَقُولِي: مَا أَحْسَنَ السَّمَاءَ! فَحِينَئِذٍ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ، وَأَوَّلُ مَا رَسَمَ مِنْهُ بَابُ التَّعَجُّبِ.
paragraphs.en: It is also related of him that Abū al-Aswad's daughter said to him: “Mā aḥsanu al-samāʾi!” (What is the most beautiful thing in the sky?) He said to her: Its stars. She said: I did not mean that; I was only wondering at its beauty. He said to her: Then say: “Mā aḥsana al-samāʾa!” (How beautiful the sky is!) It was then that he laid down grammar, and the first part of it that he drew up was the chapter of wonder.

paragraphs.ar: وَحَكَى أَبُو حَاتِمٍ السِّجِسْتَانِيُّ: وُلِدَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ، وَأَخَذَ النَّحْوَ عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ. وَرَوَى أَبُو سَلَمَةَ مُوسَى بْنُ إِسْمَاعِيلَ عَنْ أَبِيهِ قَالَ: كَانَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ بِالْبَصْرَةِ.
paragraphs.en: Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī reported: Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī was born in the Jāhiliyya, and he took grammar from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, God be pleased with him. Abū Salama Mūsā ibn Ismāʿīl related from his father: Abū al-Aswad was the first to lay down grammar in Basra.

paragraphs.ar: وَزَعَمَ قَوْمٌ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ هُرْمُزَ الْأَعْرَجُ، وَزَعَمَ آخَرُونَ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ نَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ. فَأَمَّا مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ هُرْمُزَ الْأَعْرَجُ أَوْ نَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ فَلَيْسَ بِصَحِيحٍ؛ لِأَنَّ عَبْدَ الرَّحْمٰنِ أَخَذَ عَنْ أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، وَيُقَالُ: عَنْ مَيْمُونٍ الْأَقْرَنِ. وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ؛ لِأَنَّ الرِّوَايَاتِ كُلَّهَا تُسْنَدُ إِلَى أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، وَأَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ يُسْنِدُ إِلَى عَلِيٍّ، فَإِنَّهُ رُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ فَقِيلَ لَهُ: مِنْ أَيْنَ لَكَ هٰذَا النَّحْوُ؟ فَقَالَ: لَفَّقْتُ حُدُودَهُ مِنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ.
paragraphs.en: Some claim that the first to lay down grammar was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz al-Aʿraj, and others that the first to lay down grammar was Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim. The claim that the first to lay down grammar was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz al-Aʿraj or Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim is not sound, for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān took from Abū al-Aswad, or, as some say, from Maymūn al-Aqran. What is sound is that the first to lay down grammar was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, God be pleased with him, for all the reports go back to Abū al-Aswad, and Abū al-Aswad traces it back to ʿAlī. It is related of Abū al-Aswad that he was asked: Where did you get this grammar from? He said: I pieced together its rules from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُحْكَى عَنْ يَحْيَى بْنِ مَعِينٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَاتَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ فِي الطَّاعُونِ الْجَارِفِ سَنَةَ تِسْعٍ وَسِتِّينَ. قَالَ يَحْيَى: وَيُقَالُ إِنَّهُ مَاتَ قَبْلَ الطَّاعُونِ، وَذٰلِكَ فِي خِلَافَةِ أَبِي خُبَيْبٍ عَبْدِ اللهِ بْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ. وَأَخَذَ عَنْ أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ عَنْبَسَةُ الْفِيلُ، وَمَيْمُونٌ الْأَقْرَنُ، وَنَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ هُرْمُزَ، وَيَحْيَى بْنُ يَعْمُرَ.
paragraphs.en: It is reported that Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn said: Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī died in the Sweeping Plague, in the year sixty-nine. Yaḥyā said: It is also said that he died before the plague, during the caliphate of Abū Khubayb ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr. From Abū al-Aswad took ʿAnbasa al-Fīl, Maymūn al-Aqran, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar.

The index's other sub-headings (why ʿUmar gave his order, p. 9; Abū al-Aswad with Ziyād and his daughter, p. 12; his death and pupils, p. 14) have no heading in the text and are not added. p. 3: الدُّئِل … فُعِل and مُعْرَسُهُ are vocalised so in the print. p. 6: “ما يُحْصَى عَلَيَّا” as printed (يُحصى with the print's damma). p. 7: the print repeats فلا at a line break (“ترجمون فلا / فلا تصيبون”); written once. p. 8–9: “إن يكن الله تعالى برئ من رسوله” read with the verb بَرِئَ. p. 13: the print has “عبد الرحمن بن هرمز الأعرج . بن نصر بن عاصم”; “بن” is evidently a misprint for “أو” (the sentence before names the two as separate claims), so أَوْ نَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ is written. p. 13: “لفقت حدوده” as printed, read لَفَّقْتُ (“I pieced together”). Handwritten marginal glosses on pp. 3–4 (from the Qāmūs, on الدئل/الوعل) are not part of the print and are left out.

entries.heading: عَنْبَسَةُ الْفِيلُ
entries.name: ʿAnbasa al-Fīl

paragraphs.ar: فَأَمَّا عَنْبَسَةُ الْفِيلُ فَهُوَ ابْنُ مَعْدَانَ، وَكَانَ مَعْدَانُ رَجُلًا مِنْ أَهْلِ مَيْسَانَ، قَدِمَ الْبَصْرَةَ وَأَقَامَ بِهَا، وَكَانَ يُقَالُ لَهُ مَعْدَانُ الْفِيلُ. وَسَبَبُ ذٰلِكَ أَنَّ عَبْدَ اللهِ بْنَ عَامِرٍ كَانَ لَهُ فِيلٌ بِالْبَصْرَةِ، وَقَدِ اسْتَكْثَرَ النَّفَقَةَ عَلَيْهِ، فَأَتَاهُ مَعْدَانُ فَتَقَبَّلَ نَفَقَتَهُ، وَفَضَلَ فِي كُلِّ شَهْرٍ، فَكَانَ يُدْعَى مَعْدَانَ الْفِيلِ.
paragraphs.en: As for ʿAnbasa al-Fīl (“the Elephant”), he was the son of Maʿdān. Maʿdān was a man of the people of Maysān who came to Basra and settled there, and he was called Maʿdān al-Fīl. The reason for this was that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir had an elephant in Basra and found its upkeep too costly; Maʿdān came to him and took over its upkeep, and made a profit on it every month. So he came to be called Maʿdān of the Elephant.

paragraphs.ar:
فَنَشَأَ لَهُ عَنْبَسَةُ، فَتَعَلَّمَ النَّحْوَ عَلَى أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، وَرَوَى الشِّعْرَ، وَانْتَسَبَ إِلَى مَهْرَةَ بْنِ حَيْدَانَ، وَرَوَى لِجَرِيرٍ شِعْرًا، فَبَلَغَ ذٰلِكَ الْفَرَزْدَقَ فَقَالَ يَهْجُوهُ:
لَقَدْ كَانَ فِي مَعْدَانَ وَالْفِيلِ زَاجِرٌ * لِعَنْبَسَةَ الرَّاوِي عَلَيَّ الْقَصَائِدَا
paragraphs.en: His son ʿAnbasa grew up; he learned grammar under Abū al-Aswad, transmitted poetry, and traced his descent to Mahra ibn Ḥaydān. He transmitted poetry of Jarīr, and when that reached al-Farazdaq he said, lampooning him: In Maʿdān and the elephant there was surely a warning to ʿAnbasa, who spreads poems against me.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ بَعْضَ عُمَّالِ الْبَصْرَةِ سَأَلَ عَنْبَسَةَ عَنْ هٰذَا الْبَيْتِ وَعَنِ الْفِيلِ، فَقَالَ عَنْبَسَةُ: لَمْ يَقُلِ الْفِيلَ، وَإِنَّمَا قَالَ اللُّؤْمَ. فَقَالَ لِعَنْبَسَةَ: إِنَّ أَمْرًا تَفِرُّ مِنْهُ إِلَى اللُّؤْمِ لَأَمْرٌ عَظِيمٌ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that one of the governors of Basra asked ʿAnbasa about this verse and about the elephant. ʿAnbasa said: He did not say “the elephant” (al-fīl); he said “baseness” (al-luʾm). The governor said to ʿAnbasa: A thing from which you flee to baseness must be a grave thing indeed.

paragraphs.ar: وَرُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي عُبَيْدَةَ مَعْمَرِ بْنِ الْمُثَنَّى أَنَّهُ قَالَ: اخْتَلَفَ النَّاسُ إِلَى أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيِّ يَتَعَلَّمُونَ مِنْهُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ، فَكَانَ أَبْرَعَ أَصْحَابِهِ عَنْبَسَةُ بْنُ مَعْدَانَ الْمَهْرِيُّ، وَاخْتَلَفَ النَّاسُ إِلَى عَنْبَسَةَ فَكَانَ أَبْرَعَ أَصْحَابِهِ مَيْمُونٌ الْأَقْرَنُ. وَرُوِيَ أَيْضًا عَنْ أَبِي عُبَيْدَةَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: أَوَّلُ مَنْ وَضَعَ النَّحْوَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ الدُّؤَلِيُّ، ثُمَّ مَيْمُونٌ الْأَقْرَنُ، ثُمَّ عَنْبَسَةُ الْفِيلُ، ثُمَّ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ إِسْحَاقَ، ثُمَّ عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ؛ فَفِي هٰذِهِ الرِّوَايَةِ مَيْمُونٌ الْأَقْرَنُ قَبْلَ عَنْبَسَةَ، وَفِي تِلْكَ الرِّوَايَةِ عَنْبَسَةُ قَبْلَ مَيْمُونٍ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā said: People went regularly to Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī to learn Arabic from him, and the most brilliant of his pupils was ʿAnbasa ibn Maʿdān al-Mahrī; then people went regularly to ʿAnbasa, and the most brilliant of his pupils was Maymūn al-Aqran. It is also related that Abū ʿUbayda said: The first to lay down grammar was Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, then Maymūn al-Aqran, then ʿAnbasa al-Fīl, then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Isḥāq, then ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar. In this report Maymūn al-Aqran comes before ʿAnbasa, and in the other ʿAnbasa comes before Maymūn.

entries.notes: The print sets no marginal heading for this entry (the next entries have one); the heading is the index's. died: not in the entry; no date is usually given (he lived in the generation after Abū al-Aswad, late 1st/7th century). p. 15: يَهْجُوهُ stands above فقال, in the print's own hand. p. 16: “عبد الله بن إسحاق” as printed (for Ibn Abī Isḥāq, entry 6).

entries.heading: نَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ اللَّيْثِيُّ
entries.name: Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim al-Laythī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا نَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ اللَّيْثِيُّ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ فَقِيهًا عَالِمًا بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ فَصِيحًا. قَالَ عَمْرُو بْنُ دِينَارٍ: اجْتَمَعْتُ وَالزُّهْرِيُّ وَنَصْرُ بْنُ عَاصِمٍ، فَتَكَلَّمَ نَصْرٌ، فَقَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ: إِنَّهُ لَيُفَلِّقُ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ تَفْلِيقًا.
paragraphs.en: As for Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim al-Laythī, he was a jurist, learned in Arabic and eloquent. ʿAmr ibn Dīnār said: al-Zuhrī, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and I came together, and Naṣr spoke. Al-Zuhrī said: He truly works wonders with Arabic.

paragraphs.ar:
قَالَ الْمَدَائِنِيُّ: وَكَانَ يَرَى رَأْيَ الْخَوَارِجِ، ثُمَّ تَرَكَهُمْ وَرَجَعَ عَنْهُ، وَقَالَ فِي ذٰلِكَ:
فَارَقْتُ نَجْدَةَ وَالَّذِينَ تَزَرَّقُوا * وَابْنَ الزُّبَيْرِ وَشِيعَةَ الْكَذَّابِ
وَهَوَى النَّجَّارِيِّينَ قَدْ فَارَقْتُهُ * وَعَطِيَّةِ الْمُتَجَبِّرِ الْمُرْتَابِ
paragraphs.en: Al-Madāʾinī said: He used to hold the views of the Khārijites; then he left them and turned back from it, and he said on this: I have parted from Najda and those who became Azraqites, from Ibn al-Zubayr and the party of the Liar; and the leaning towards the Najjāriyya I have left, and towards ʿAṭiyya, the overbearing, the doubter.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَرَأَ الْقُرْآنَ أَيْضًا عَلَى أَبِي الْأَسْوَدِ، وَقَرَأَ أَبُو الْأَسْوَدِ عَلَى عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ، فَكَانَ أُسْتَاذَهُ فِي الْقِرَاءَةِ وَالنَّحْوِ. وَمَاتَ سَنَةَ تِسْعٍ وَثَمَانِينَ فِي أَيَّامِ الْوَلِيدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ، وَيُقَالُ: إِنَّهُ مَاتَ بِالْبَصْرَةِ سَنَةَ تِسْعِينَ فِي أَيَّامِ الْوَلِيدِ.
paragraphs.en: He also read the Qurʾān with Abū al-Aswad, and Abū al-Aswad read with ʿAlī, God be pleased with him; so he was his master both in Qurʾān reading and in grammar. He died in the year eighty-nine, in the days of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik; it is also said that he died in Basra in the year ninety, in the days of al-Walīd.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “نصر بن عاصم الليثي”. p. 17: the rhyme word of the first verse looks like “الكرّابى” in the print; read الْكَذَّابِ (the party of al-Mukhtār), which the sense and the rhyme require. In the second verse عَطِيَّةِ is read as governed by هَوَى (genitive), which keeps the rhyme.

entries.heading: أَبُو دَاوُدَ الْأَعْرَجُ
entries.name: Abū Dāwūd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz al-Aʿraj

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا الْأَعْرَجُ فَهُوَ أَبُو دَاوُدَ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ هُرْمُزَ الْأَعْرَجُ، وَكَانَ مَوْلًى لِمُحَمَّدِ بْنِ رَبِيعَةَ بْنِ الْحَارِثِ بْنِ الْمُطَّلِبِ، وَكَانَ أَحَدَ الْقُرَّاءِ، عَالِمًا بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ، وَأَعْلَمَ النَّاسِ بِأَنْسَابِ الْعَرَبِ، وَخَرَجَ إِلَى الْإِسْكَنْدَرِيَّةِ وَأَقَامَ بِهَا إِلَى أَنْ مَاتَ سَنَةَ سَبْعَ عَشْرَةَ فِي أَيَّامِ هِشَامِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ.
paragraphs.en: As for al-Aʿraj, he is Abū Dāwūd ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hurmuz al-Aʿraj. He was a client of Muḥammad ibn Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Muṭṭalib; he was one of the Qurʾān readers, learned in Arabic, and the most learned of men in the genealogies of the Arabs. He went out to Alexandria and stayed there until he died in the year seventeen, in the days of Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “أبو داود الأعرج”. “سنة سبع عشرة” as printed; the hundred is left out (Hishām reigned 105–125, so 117/735 is meant).

entries.heading: يَحْيَى بْنُ يَعْمُرَ الْعَدْوَانِيُّ
entries.name: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar al-ʿAdwānī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا يَحْيَى بْنُ يَعْمُرَ الْعَدْوَانِيُّ فَيُكْنَى أَبَا سُلَيْمَانَ، وَهُوَ رَجُلٌ مِنْ عَدْوَانَ بْنِ قَيْسِ بْنِ عَيْلَانَ مِنْ مُضَرَ، وَكَانَ عَالِمًا بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ، وَلَقِيَ عَبْدَ اللهِ بْنَ عُمَرَ وَعَبْدَ اللهِ بْنَ عَبَّاسٍ وَغَيْرَهُمَا مِنَ الصَّحَابَةِ، وَرَوَى عَنْهُ قَتَادَةُ، وَكَانَ مِنَ الْفُصَحَاءِ.
paragraphs.en: As for Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar al-ʿAdwānī, his kunya was Abū Sulaymān. He was a man of ʿAdwān ibn Qays ibn ʿAylān, of Muḍar. He was learned in Arabic and in ḥadīth; he met ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and other Companions, and Qatāda transmitted from him. He was one of the eloquent.

paragraphs.ar: وَكَانَ قَدْ وَلَّاهُ يَزِيدُ بْنُ الْمُهَلَّبِ الْقَضَاءَ بِخُرَاسَانَ، فَقَالَ لَهُ يَوْمًا: هَلْ تَشْرَبُ النَّبِيذَ؟ فَقَالَ: مَا أَدَعُهُ فِي صَبَاحِي وَمَسَائِي. فَقَالَ لَهُ: أَنْتَ وَنَبِيذُكَ. وَعَزَلَهُ عَنِ الْقَضَاءِ.
paragraphs.en: Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab had made him judge in Khurasan. One day he said to him: Do you drink nabīdh? He said: I do not leave it, morning or evening. He said to him: Then you and your nabīdh! And he removed him from the judgeship.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ الْحَجَّاجَ بْنَ يُوسُفَ قَالَ لَهُ: أَتَجِدُنِي أَلْحَنُ؟ فَقَالَ: الْأَمِيرُ أَفْصَحُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ. فَقَالَ: عَزَمْتُ عَلَيْكَ، أَتَجِدُنِي أَلْحَنُ؟ فَقَالَ يَحْيَى: نَعَمْ. فَقَالَ لَهُ: فِي أَيِّ شَيْءٍ؟ فَقَالَ: فِي كِتَابِ اللهِ تَعَالَى. فَقَالَ: ذٰلِكَ أَشْنَعُ، فَفِي أَيِّ شَيْءٍ مِنْ كِتَابِ اللهِ تَعَالَى؟ قَالَ: قَرَأْتَ: «قُلْ إِنْ كَانَ آبَاؤُكُمْ وَأَبْنَاؤُكُمْ وَإِخْوَانُكُمْ وَأَزْوَاجُكُمْ وَعَشِيرَتُكُمْ وَأَمْوَالٌ اقْتَرَفْتُمُوهَا وَتِجَارَةٌ تَخْشَوْنَ كَسَادَهَا وَمَسَاكِنُ تَرْضَوْنَهَا أَحَبُّ إِلَيْكُمْ»، فَرَفَعْتَ أَحَبَّ وَهُوَ مَنْصُوبٌ. فَقَالَ لَهُ الْحَجَّاجُ: طُولُ لِحْيَتِكَ أَوْقَعَكَ. وَكَانَ طَوِيلَ اللِّحْيَةِ. فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ مِمَّنْ حَضَرَ: أَيُّهَا الْأَمِيرُ، حَدَّثَنِي كَعْبُ الْأَحْبَارِ أَنَّهُ مَكْتُوبٌ فِي بَعْضِ الْكُتُبِ أَنَّ اللِّحْيَةَ مَخْرَجُهَا مِنَ الدِّمَاغِ، فَمَنْ تُفْرِطُ عَلَيْهِ لِحْيَتُهُ فِي طُولِهَا تَخِفُّ دِمَاغُهُ، وَمَنْ خَفَّ دِمَاغُهُ قَلَّ عَقْلُهُ، وَمَنْ قَلَّ عَقْلُهُ كَانَ أَحْمَقَ، وَالْأَحْمَقُ لَا يُسْمَعُ مِنْهُ. فَقَالَ الْحَجَّاجُ: لَا تُسَاكِنِّي بِبَلَدٍ أَنَا فِيهِ. وَنَفَاهُ إِلَى خُرَاسَانَ، وَبِهَا يَزِيدُ بْنُ الْمُهَلَّبِ، فَكَانَ عِنْدَهُ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf said to him: Do you find that I make mistakes in my Arabic? He said: The governor is too eloquent for that. He said: I adjure you: do you find that I make mistakes? Yaḥyā said: Yes. He said to him: In what? He said: In the Book of God, exalted is He. He said: That is worse. In what part of the Book of God, exalted is He? He said: You recited: “Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose slackness you fear, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer (aḥabbu) to you …”, and you put aḥabb in the nominative when it is in the accusative. Al-Ḥajjāj said to him: The length of your beard has made you fall into this. He had a long beard. A man among those present said: Governor, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār told me that it is written in one of the books that the beard grows out of the brain, so whoever lets his beard grow too long, his brain grows light; whoever's brain is light has little sense; whoever has little sense is a fool; and a fool is not to be listened to. Al-Ḥajjāj said: Do not live with me in a town where I am. He banished him to Khurasan, where Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab was, and he stayed with him.

paragraphs.ar: قَالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سَلَّامٍ: أَخْبَرَنِي أَبِي أَنَّ يَزِيدَ بْنَ الْمُهَلَّبِ كَتَبَ إِلَى الْحَجَّاجِ: إِنَّا لَقِينَا الْعَدُوَّ فَفَعَلْنَا وَفَعَلْنَا، وَاضْطَرَرْنَا إِلَى عُرْعُرَةِ الْجَبَلِ. فَقَالَ الْحَجَّاجُ: مَا لِابْنِ الْمُهَلَّبِ وَهٰذَا الْكَلَامِ! فَقِيلَ لَهُ: إِنَّ يَحْيَى بْنَ يَعْمُرَ عِنْدَهُ. فَقَالَ: فَذَاكَ إِذَنْ.
paragraphs.en: Muḥammad ibn Sallām said: My father told me that Yazīd ibn al-Muhallab wrote to al-Ḥajjāj: We met the enemy and did this and that, and drove them up to the very peak (ʿurʿura) of the mountain. Al-Ḥajjāj said: What has Ibn al-Muhallab to do with language like this? He was told: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar is with him. He said: That explains it, then.

paragraphs.ar: وَكَانَ يَسْتَعْمِلُ الْغَرِيبَ فِي كَلَامِهِ، فَمِنْ ذٰلِكَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِرَجُلٍ خَاصَمَتْهُ امْرَأَتُهُ: أَإِنْ سَأَلَتْكَ ثَمَنَ شَكْرِهَا وَسِرِّكَ أَنْشَأْتَ تَمْطُلُهَا وَتَضْهَلُهَا؟ الشَّكْرُ: الْفَرْجُ، وَالسِّرُّ: النِّكَاحُ، وَيُرْوَى: وَشَبْرِكَ، وَالشَّبْرُ: الْعَطَاءُ. وَخَاصَمَ رَجُلٌ رَجُلًا فِي غُلَامٍ، فَقَالَ: بَاعَنِي غُلَامًا آبِقًا، فَقَالَ لَهُ يَحْيَى: أَلَا قُلْتَ: أَبُوقًا؟
paragraphs.en: He used rare words in his speech. For example, he said to a man whose wife had brought a suit against him: When she asks you for the price of her shakr and your sirr, do you start putting her off and paying her out in driblets? Shakr is the private part and sirr is intercourse; it is also related as “and your shabr”, shabr being a gift. And when a man disputed with another over a slave, saying: He sold me a runaway (ābiq) slave, Yaḥyā said to him: Why did you not say: an habitual runaway (abūq)?

paragraphs.ar: وَمَاتَ يَحْيَى بْنُ يَعْمُرَ بِخُرَاسَانَ سَنَةَ تِسْعٍ وَعِشْرِينَ وَمِائَةٍ فِي أَيَّامِ مَرْوَانَ بْنِ مُحَمَّدٍ.
paragraphs.en: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar died in Khurasan in the year one hundred and twenty-nine, in the days of Marwān ibn Muḥammad.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “يحيى بن يعمر العدواني”; the print vowels the name يَعْمُر (with ḍamma on the mīm), kept in the Arabic. p. 21: the print spells تخف دماغه (feminine) and “واضطررنا إلى عرعرة الجبل” without an object; both as printed. p. 21: “ثمن شكرها وسرك” as printed (وَسِرِّك; the print itself then gives the variant وَشَبْرِك).

entries.heading: ابْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ
entries.name: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا ابْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ فَهُوَ أَبُو بَحْرٍ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ الْحَضْرَمِيُّ، وَكَانَ قَيِّمًا بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ، إِمَامًا فِيهِمَا، وَكَانَ شَدِيدَ التَّجْرِيدِ لِلْقِيَاسِ، وَيُقَالُ: إِنَّهُ كَانَ أَشَدَّ تَجْرِيدًا لِلْقِيَاسِ مِنْ أَبِي عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَلَاءِ، وَكَانَ أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ أَوْسَعَ عِلْمًا بِكَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ وَلُغَاتِهَا وَغَرِيبِهَا. وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ بِلَالَ بْنَ أَبِي بُرْدَةَ جَمَعَ بَيْنَهُمَا، قَالَ يُونُسُ: قَالَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو: فَغَلَبَنِي ابْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِالْهَمْزِ، فَنَظَرْتُ فِيهِ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ. وَيُقَالُ: إِنَّهُ أَوَّلُ مَنْ عَلَّلَ النَّحْوَ.
paragraphs.en: As for Ibn Abī Isḥāq, he is Abū Baḥr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī. He was a master of Arabic and of Qurʾān reading and a leading authority in both. He held strictly to pure analogy (qiyās); it is said that he held to analogy more strictly than Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, while Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ had the wider knowledge of the speech of the Arabs, their dialects and their rare words. It is related that Bilāl ibn Abī Burda brought the two of them together. Yūnus said: Abū ʿAmr said: Ibn Abī Isḥāq got the better of me that day over the hamza, and afterwards I studied it. It is said that he was the first to give the reasons (ʿilal) of grammar.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سَلَّامٍ: سَمِعْتُ رَجُلًا يَسْأَلُ يُونُسَ عَنْ عَبْدِ اللهِ بْنِ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ وَعِلْمِهِ، فَقَالَ: هُوَ وَالْبَحْرُ سَوَاءٌ، أَيْ: هُوَ الْغَايَةُ. وَقَالَ يُونُسُ: كَانَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو أَشَدَّ النَّاسِ تَسْلِيمًا لِلْعَرَبِ، وَكَانَ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ وَعِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ يَطْعَنَانِ عَلَى الْعَرَبِ.
paragraphs.en: Muḥammad ibn Sallām said: I heard a man ask Yūnus about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq and his learning. He said: He and the sea are alike, that is, he is the utmost. Yūnus said: Abū ʿAmr was of all men the readiest to accept what the Arabs said, while ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar would find fault with the Arabs.

paragraphs.ar:
وَكَانَ مَوَالِي ابْنِ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ الْحَضْرَمِيِّ مَوَالِيَ، وَهُمْ حُلَفَاءُ فِي بَنِي عَبْدِ شَمْسِ بْنِ عَبْدِ مَنَافٍ، وَكَانَ يَرُدُّ كَثِيرًا عَلَى الْفَرَزْدَقِ وَيُكَلِّمُهُ فِي شِعْرِهِ، فَقَالَ فِيهِ الْفَرَزْدَقُ:
فَلَوْ كَانَ عَبْدُ اللهِ مَوْلًى هَجَوْتُهُ * وَلٰكِنَّ عَبْدَ اللهِ مَوْلَى مَوَالِيَا
فَقَالَ لَهُ ابْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ: وَلَقَدْ لَحَنْتَ أَيْضًا فِي قَوْلِكَ: مَوْلَى مَوَالِيَا، وَكَانَ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ تَقُولَ: مَوْلَى مَوَالٍ. وَالْحَلِيفُ عِنْدَ الْعَرَبِ مَوْلًى، وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُ الْأَخْطَلِ:
أَلَسْتُمْ قَوْمًا أَثْبَتُوكُمْ بِنَهْشَلٍ * وَلَوْلَاهُمُ كُنْتُمْ لِعُكْلٍ مَوَالِيَا
paragraphs.en: The patrons of Ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī were themselves clients: they were confederates among the Banū ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf. He often contradicted al-Farazdaq and took him to task over his poetry, and al-Farazdaq said of him: Were ʿAbd Allāh a client, I would have lampooned him; but ʿAbd Allāh is a client of clients (mawlā mawāliyā). Ibn Abī Isḥāq said to him: You have made a mistake here too, in saying mawlā mawāliyā; you should have said mawlā mawālin. Among the Arabs a confederate is a mawlā; hence the words of al-Akhṭal: Are you not a people whom they established through Nahshal? Were it not for them, you would be clients of ʿUkl.

paragraphs.ar:
وَرَوَى أَبُو عَمْرٍو أَنَّ ابْنَ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ سَمِعَ الْفَرَزْدَقَ يُنْشِدُ:
وَعَضُّ زَمَانٍ يَا ابْنَ مَرْوَانَ لَمْ يَدَعْ * مِنَ الْمَالِ إِلَّا مُسْحَتًا أَوْ مُجَلَّفُ
فَقَالَ لَهُ ابْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ: عَلَى أَيِّ شَيْءٍ تَرْفَعُ «أَوْ مُجَلَّفُ»؟ فَقَالَ: عَلَى مَا يَسُوءُكَ وَيَنُوءُكَ. قَالَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو: فَقُلْتُ لِلْفَرَزْدَقِ: أَصَبْتَ، وَهُوَ جَائِزٌ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى، أَيْ: لَمْ يَبْقَ سِوَاهُ.
paragraphs.en: Abū ʿAmr related that Ibn Abī Isḥāq heard al-Farazdaq recite: And the bite of a time, Ibn Marwān, that has left of wealth nothing but what is destroyed (musḥatan), or a remnant (aw mujallafu). Ibn Abī Isḥāq said to him: On what ground do you put “aw mujallafu” in the nominative? He said: On the ground of what will vex you and weigh you down! Abū ʿAmr said: I said to al-Farazdaq: You are right; it is allowable by the sense, that is: nothing remained but it.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَرَأَ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ الْحَضْرَمِيُّ عَلَى يَحْيَى بْنِ يَعْمُرَ، وَقَرَأَ أَيْضًا هُوَ وَأَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ عَلَى نَصْرِ بْنِ عَاصِمٍ، وَكَانَا رَفِيقَيْنِ، وَكَانَ هُوَ وَأَبُو عَمْرٍو وَعِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ فِي وَقْتٍ وَاحِدٍ، وَتُوُفِّيَ قَبْلَهُمَا بِالْبَصْرَةِ سَنَةَ سَبْعَ عَشْرَةَ وَمِائَةٍ فِي أَيَّامِ هِشَامِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ.
paragraphs.en: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī read the Qurʾān with Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar; he and Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ also read with Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, and the two were companions. He, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar lived at the same time, and he died before the other two, in Basra, in the year one hundred and seventeen, in the days of Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “ابن أبي إسحاق” (written beside p. 22). p. 23: “وكان موالي ابن أبي إسحاق الحضرمي مواليا” as printed (the second word spelt with a final alif); vocalised مَوَالِيَ. Handwritten marginal glosses on pp. 22 and 24 are not part of the print.

entries.heading: عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ الثَّقَفِيُّ
entries.name: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ الثَّقَفِيُّ فَكُنْيَتُهُ أَبُو سُلَيْمَانَ، وَيُقَالُ: أَبُو عَمْرٍو، وَكَانَ ثِقَةً عَالِمًا بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالنَّحْوِ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ، وَقِرَاءَتُهُ مَشْهُورَةٌ، وَكَانَ فَصِيحًا يَتَقَعَّرُ فِي كَلَامِهِ، وَيَعْدِلُ عَنْ سَهْلِ الْأَلْفَاظِ إِلَى الْوَحْشِيِّ وَالْغَرِيبِ.
paragraphs.en: As for ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafī, his kunya was Abū Sulaymān, or, as some say, Abū ʿAmr. He was trustworthy, learned in Arabic, grammar and Qurʾān reading, and his reading is well known. He was eloquent, but spoke affectedly, from the back of his throat, turning from plain words to uncouth and rare ones.

paragraphs.ar: فَمِنْ ذٰلِكَ أَنَّهُ لَمَّا ضَرَبَهُ يُوسُفُ بْنُ عُمَرَ بْنِ هُبَيْرَةَ فِي سَبَبِ ثِيَابٍ اسْتُودِعَهَا قَالَ: إِنْ كَانَتْ إِلَّا أُثَيَّابًا فِي أُسَيْفَاطٍ قَبَضَهَا عَشَّارُوكَ. وَذٰلِكَ أَنَّ بَعْضَ أَصْحَابِ خَالِدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللهِ الْقَسْرِيِّ أَوْدَعَهُ وَدِيعَةً، فَلَمَّا نُزِعَ خَالِدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللهِ عَنْ إِمَارَةِ الْعِرَاقِ، وَتَقَلَّدَ مَكَانَهُ يُوسُفُ بْنُ عُمَرَ، كَتَبَ إِلَى وَالِيهِ بِالْبَصْرَةِ أَنْ يَحْمِلَ إِلَيْهِ عِيسَى بْنَ عُمَرَ مُقَيَّدًا، فَدَعَا بِهِ، وَدَعَا بِالْحَدَّادِ، وَأَمَرَهُ بِتَقْيِيدِهِ، وَقَالَ: لَا بَأْسَ عَلَيْكَ، إِنَّمَا أَرَادَ الْأَمِيرُ أَنْ يُؤَدِّبَ وَلَدَهُ. قَالَ: فَمَا بَالُ الْقَيْدِ إِذَنْ؟ فَبَقِيَتْ مَثَلًا بِالْبَصْرَةِ. فَلَمَّا أُتِيَ بِهِ يُوسُفُ بْنُ عُمَرَ سَأَلَهُ عَنِ الْوَدِيعَةِ فَأَنْكَرَهَا، فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَضُرِبَ بِالسِّيَاطِ، فَلَمَّا أَخَذَهُ السَّوْطُ جَزِعَ، فَقَالَ: أَيُّهَا الْأَمِيرُ، وَاللهِ إِنْ كَانَتْ إِلَّا أُثَيَّابًا فِي أُسَيْفَاطٍ قَبَضَهَا عَشَّارُوكَ. فَرُفِعَ السَّوْطُ عَنْهُ، وَوُكِّلَ بِهِ حَتَّى أُخِذَتِ الْوَدِيعَةُ مِنْهُ.
paragraphs.en: For example, when Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar ibn Hubayra had him flogged on account of some clothes that had been deposited with him, he said: They were nothing but some little clothes in some little baskets, which your tithe-collectors took. This was because one of the men of Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī had left a deposit with him. When Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh was removed from the governorship of Iraq and Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar took his place, he wrote to his governor in Basra to send him ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar in fetters. The governor summoned him, summoned the smith, and ordered him to be fettered, saying: No harm will come to you; the governor only wants you to teach his son. He said: Then why the fetters? This became a proverb in Basra. When he was brought to Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar, he asked him about the deposit and he denied it, so he ordered him to be flogged. When the whip took hold of him he could not bear it, and said: Governor, by God, they were nothing but some little clothes in some little baskets, which your tithe-collectors took. The whip was lifted from him, and he was kept under guard until the deposit was taken from him.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ سُلَيْمَانَ: رَأَيْتُ عِيسَى بْنَ عُمَرَ طُولَ دَهْرِهِ يَحْمِلُ فِي كُمِّهِ خِرْقَةً فِيهَا سُكَّرُ الْعُشَرِ وَالْإِجَّاصُ الْيَابِسُ، وَرُبَّمَا رَأَيْتُهُ وَاقِفًا عِنْدِي أَوْ سَائِرًا، وَعِنْدَ وُلَاةِ أَهْلِ الْبَصْرَةِ، فَتُصِيبُهُ نَهْكَةٌ عَلَى فُؤَادِهِ، فَيَخْفِقُ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّى يَكَادَ يُغْلَبُ، فَيَسْتَغِيثُ بِإِجَّاصَةٍ وَسُكَّرٍ يُلْقِيهِمَا فِي فَمِهِ ثُمَّ يَمْتَصُّهُمَا، فَإِذَا ازْدَرَدَ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ شَيْئًا سَكَنَ عَلَيْهِ، فَسَأَلْتُهُ عَنْ ذٰلِكَ فَقَالَ: أَصَابَنِي هٰذَا مِنَ الضَّرْبِ الَّذِي ضَرَبَنِي يُوسُفُ بْنُ عُمَرَ، فَعَالَجْتُهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ فَلَمْ أَجِدْ لَهُ أَصْلَحَ مِنْ هٰذَا.
paragraphs.en: ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān said: All his life I saw ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar carry in his sleeve a rag holding ʿushar sugar and dried plums. Sometimes I saw him standing with me or walking, or with the governors of the people of Basra, when a weakness would seize him at the heart, and his heart would flutter until he was almost overcome; then he would seek relief in a plum and some sugar, which he put in his mouth and sucked, and when he had swallowed some of it, he grew calm. I asked him about this, and he said: This came upon me from the flogging Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar gave me. I have treated it with everything, and have found nothing better for it than this.

paragraphs.ar:
وَصَنَّفَ كِتَابَيْنِ فِي النَّحْوِ سَمَّى أَحَدَهُمَا الْجَامِعَ، وَالْآخَرَ الْإِكْمَالَ، وَفِيهِمَا يَقُولُ الْخَلِيلُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ، وَكَانَ الْخَلِيلُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ قَدْ أَخَذَ عَنْهُ:
ذَهَبَ النَّحْوُ جَمِيعًا كُلُّهُ * غَيْرَ مَا أَحْدَثَ عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرْ
ذَاكَ إِكْمَالٌ وَهٰذَا جَامِعٌ * فَهُمَا لِلنَّاسِ شَمْسٌ وَقَمَرْ
وَهٰذَانِ الْكِتَابَانِ لَمْ نَرَهُمَا، وَلَمْ نَرَ أَحَدًا رَآهُمَا.
paragraphs.en: He composed two books on grammar, one of which he called al-Jāmiʿ (The Comprehensive) and the other al-Ikmāl (The Completion). Of them al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, who had studied with him, says: All grammar has gone, all of it, except what ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar brought forth: that is a Completion and this a Comprehensive, and the two are a sun and a moon for mankind. We have not seen these two books, nor have we seen anyone who has seen them.

paragraphs.ar:
وَقَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ الْمُبَارَكِ الْيَزِيدِيُّ:
يَا طَالِبَ النَّحْوِ أَلَا فَابْكِهِ * بَعْدَ أَبِي عَمْرٍو وَحَمَّادِ
وَابْنِ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ فِي عِلْمِهِ * وَالزَّيْنِ فِي الْمَشْهَدِ وَالنَّادِي
عِيسَى وَأَشْبَاهٍ لِعِيسَى وَهَلْ * يَأْتِي لَهُمْ دَهْرٌ بِأَنْدَادِ
وَيُونُسَ النَّحْوِيَّ لَا تَنْسَهُ * وَلَا خَلِيلًا حَيَّةَ الْوَادِي
paragraphs.en: Yaḥyā ibn al-Mubārak al-Yazīdī said: Seeker of grammar, weep for it, now that Abū ʿAmr and Ḥammād are gone, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq in his learning, and the ornament of every gathering and assembly, ʿĪsā, and men like ʿĪsā; will time ever bring their equals? And do not forget Yūnus the grammarian, nor Khalīl, the serpent of the valley.

paragraphs.ar: وَتُوُفِّيَ سَنَةَ تِسْعٍ وَأَرْبَعِينَ وَمِائَةٍ، وَيَشْهَدُ لِهٰذَا مَا رُوِيَ عَنِ الْأَصْمَعِيِّ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: تُوُفِّيَ عِيسَى بْنُ عُمَرَ قَبْلَ أَبِي عَمْرٍو بِخَمْسِ سِنِينَ، وَكَانَ ذٰلِكَ فِي خِلَافَةِ أَبِي جَعْفَرٍ الْمَنْصُورِ، وَتُوُفِّيَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو سَنَةَ أَرْبَعٍ وَخَمْسِينَ وَمِائَةٍ عَلَى مَا سَنَذْكُرُهُ إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ تَعَالَى.
paragraphs.en: He died in the year one hundred and forty-nine. This is borne out by what is related of al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar died five years before Abū ʿAmr, during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr; and Abū ʿAmr died in the year one hundred and fifty-four, as we shall mention, God willing.

entries.heading: أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ
entries.name: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ

paragraphs.ar:
وَأَمَّا أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ فَهُوَ الْعَلَمُ الْمَشْهُورُ فِي عِلْمِ الْقِرَاءَةِ وَاللُّغَةِ وَالْعَرَبِيَّةِ، وَكَانَ مِنَ الشَّأْنِ بِمَكَانٍ، وَاسْمُهُ زَبَّانُ. وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ الْفَرَزْدَقَ جَاءَ مُعْتَذِرًا إِلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْلِ هَجْوٍ بَلَغَهُ عَنْهُ، فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو عَمْرٍو:
هَجَوْتَ زَبَّانَ ثُمَّ جِئْتَ مُعْتَذِرًا * مِنْ هَجْوِ زَبَّانَ لَمْ تَهْجُو وَلَمْ تَدَعِ
فَهٰذَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ اسْمَهُ زَبَّانُ، وَاخْتَلَفُوا فِي اسْمِهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا، وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَالَ: اسْمُهُ كُنْيَتُهُ.
paragraphs.en: As for Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, he is the famous authority in the science of Qurʾān reading, lexicography and Arabic, and he held a high place in the field. His name was Zabbān. It is related that al-Farazdaq came to him to apologise for a lampoon of him that had reached him, and Abū ʿAmr said to him: You lampooned Zabbān, then came to apologise for lampooning Zabbān: you have neither lampooned nor let it be. This shows that his name was Zabbān. People have disagreed a great deal about his name; some say that his name was his kunya.

paragraphs.ar: أَخَذَ النَّحْوَ عَنْ نَصْرِ بْنِ عَاصِمٍ اللَّيْثِيِّ، وَأَخَذَ عَنْهُ يُونُسُ بْنُ حَبِيبٍ الْبَصْرِيُّ، وَالْخَلِيلُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ، وَأَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ عَلِيُّ بْنُ الْمُبَارَكِ الْيَزِيدِيُّ. وَكَانَ يُونُسُ بْنُ حَبِيبٍ يَقُولُ: لَوْ كَانَ أَحَدٌ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يُؤْخَذَ بِقَوْلِهِ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ، كَانَ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يُؤْخَذَ بِقَوْلِ أَبِي عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَلَاءِ كُلِّهِ فِي الْعَرَبِيَّةِ، وَلٰكِنْ لَيْسَ مِنْ أَحَدٍ إِلَّا وَأَنْتَ آخِذٌ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَتَارِكٌ، إِلَّا النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
paragraphs.en: He took grammar from Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim al-Laythī, and from him took Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb al-Baṣrī, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad and Abū Muḥammad ʿAlī ibn al-Mubārak al-Yazīdī. Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb used to say: If there were anyone whose word ought to be accepted in everything, the word of Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ought to be accepted, all of it, in Arabic; but there is no one from whose words you do not take some and leave some, except the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace.

paragraphs.ar: وَرَوَى الْأَصْمَعِيُّ عَنِ الْخَلِيلِ بْنِ أَحْمَدَ عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَلَاءِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: أَكْثَرُ مَنْ تَزَنْدَقَ بِالْعِرَاقِ لِجَهْلِهِمْ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ.
paragraphs.en: Al-Aṣmaʿī related from al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ that he said: Most of those who became heretics (zanādiqa) in Iraq did so through their ignorance of Arabic.

paragraphs.ar: وَحَكَى الْأَصْمَعِيُّ قَالَ: غَدَوْتُ ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ إِلَى زِيَارَةِ صَدِيقٍ لِي، فَلَقِيَنِي أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ، فَقَالَ لِي: إِلَى أَيْنَ يَا أَصْمَعِيُّ؟ قُلْتُ: إِلَى صَدِيقٍ لِي. فَقَالَ: إِنْ كَانَ لِفَائِدَةٍ، أَوْ لِمَائِدَةٍ، أَوْ لِعَائِدَةٍ، وَإِلَّا فَلَا.
paragraphs.en: Al-Aṣmaʿī reported: One morning I set out to visit a friend of mine, and Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ met me and said: Where to, Aṣmaʿī? I said: To a friend of mine. He said: If it is for some profit, or for a meal, or for a favour, well and good; if not, then no.

paragraphs.ar:
وَرُوِيَ أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ عَنْ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: «فَعَزَّزْنَا بِثَالِثٍ»، فَقَالَ: الْمَعْنَى شَدَّدْنَا، وَأَنْشَدَ:
أُجُدٌ إِذَا أُضْمِرَتْ تَعَزَّزَ لَحْمُهَا * وَإِذَا تُشَدُّ بِنِسْعِهَا لَا تَنْبِسُ
تَعَزَّزَ: أَيِ اشْتَدَّ، لَا تَنْبِسُ: لَا تُصَوِّتُ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that he was asked about the words of God, exalted is He, “so We strengthened them (ʿazzaznā) with a third”, and he said: The meaning is “We made strong”; and he recited: A sturdy she-camel: when she is trained lean her flesh grows firm (taʿazzaza), and when she is bound with her girth she makes no sound (lā tanbisu). Taʿazzaza means it became firm; lā tanbisu means she does not make a sound.

paragraphs.ar:
وَيُرْوَى عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرٍو قَالَ: كُنْتُ هَارِبًا مِنَ الْحَجَّاجِ بْنِ يُوسُفَ، وَكَانَ يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَيَّ «فَرْجَةٌ»: هَلْ هُوَ بِالْفَتْحِ أَوْ بِالضَّمِّ؟ فَسَمِعْتُ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ:
رُبَّمَا تَجْزَعُ النُّفُوسُ مِنَ الْأَمْ * رِ لَهُ فَرْجَةٌ كَحَلِّ الْعِقَالِ
بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ مِنْ فَرْجَةٍ، ثُمَّ قَالَ: أَلَا إِنَّهُ قَدْ مَاتَ الْحَجَّاجُ. قَالَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو: فَمَا أَدْرِي بِأَيِّهِمَا كُنْتُ أَشَدَّ فَرَحًا: بِقَوْلِهِ فَرْجَةٌ، أَوْ بِقَوْلِهِ مَاتَ الْحَجَّاجُ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that Abū ʿAmr said: I was in flight from al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, and I was unsure about farja (relief): was it with a or with u? Then I heard someone say: Often souls are distressed at a thing that has a relief (farja) like the loosing of a hobble — with a after the f of farja. Then he said: Hear! Al-Ḥajjāj has died. Abū ʿAmr said: I do not know which of the two gave me the greater joy: his saying farja, or his saying that al-Ḥajjāj had died.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُرْوَى أَنَّ أَبَا عَمْرٍو سَأَلَ أَبَا خَيْرَةَ عَنْ قَوْلِهِمْ: اسْتَأْصَلَ اللهُ عِرْقَاتَهُمْ، فَنَصَبَ أَبُو خَيْرَةَ التَّاءَ مِنْ عِرْقَاتِهِمْ، فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو عَمْرٍو: هَيْهَاتَ يَا أَبَا خَيْرَةَ، لَانَ جِلْدُكَ. وَذٰلِكَ أَنَّ أَبَا عَمْرٍو اسْتَضْعَفَ النَّصْبَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ سَمِعَهَا مِنْهُ بِالْجَرِّ، وَكَانَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ يَرْوِيهَا بِالنَّصْبِ وَالْجَرِّ.
paragraphs.en: It is related that Abū ʿAmr asked Abū Khayra about the saying “May God tear out their roots (ʿirqātahum)”, and Abū Khayra gave the t of ʿirqātahum an a. Abū ʿAmr said to him: Far from it, Abū Khayra; your skin has gone soft! For Abū ʿAmr thought the a weak, having heard it from him earlier with an i. Afterwards Abū ʿAmr used to transmit it both with a and with i.

paragraphs.ar:
وَكَانَ يَقُولُ: إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ بِالْإِضَافَةِ إِلَى مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَنَا كَبَقْلٍ فِي أُصُولِ رُقْلٍ، أَيْ: نَخْلٍ طِوَالٍ. وَهٰذَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَمَالِهِ فِي فَضْلِهِ، قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ:
وَمَا عَبَّرَ الْإِنْسَانُ عَنْ فَضْلِ نَفْسِهِ * بِمِثْلِ اعْتِقَادِ الْفَضْلِ فِي كُلِّ فَاضِلِ
وَإِنَّ أَشَدَّ النَّقْصِ أَنْ يَرْمِيَ الْفَتَى * قَذَى الْعَيْبِ عَنْهُ بِانْتِقَاصِ الْأَفَاضِلِ
paragraphs.en: He used to say: Compared with those before us, we are only like herbs at the foot of raql, that is, of tall palms. This shows how complete his excellence was. The poet says: A man shows his own excellence by nothing so well as by recognising the excellence of every excellent man; and the worst of failings is for a man to throw the speck of fault off himself by belittling the excellent.

paragraphs.ar: وَحَكَى يُونُسُ بْنُ حَبِيبٍ الْبَصْرِيُّ عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرٍو أَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَا انْتَهَى إِلَيْكُمْ مِمَّا قَالَتِ الْعَرَبُ إِلَّا أَقَلُّهُ، وَلَوْ جَاءَكُمْ وَافِرًا لَجَاءَكُمْ عِلْمٌ وَشِعْرٌ كَثِيرٌ.
paragraphs.en: Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb al-Baṣrī reported that Abū ʿAmr said: Only the least part of what the Arabs said has come down to you; had it come to you in full, much learning and poetry would have come to you.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْحَرْبِيُّ: كَانَ أَهْلُ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ كُلُّهُمْ أَصْحَابَ أَهْوَاءٍ إِلَّا أَرْبَعَةً، فَإِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا أَصْحَابَ سُنَّةٍ: أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ، وَالْخَلِيلُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ، وَيُونُسُ بْنُ حَبِيبٍ الْبَصْرِيُّ، وَالْأَصْمَعِيُّ.
paragraphs.en: Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī said: The men of Arabic were all followers of sectarian views except four, who were men of the Sunna: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb al-Baṣrī and al-Aṣmaʿī.

paragraphs.ar:
وَمِمَّا رُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرٍو لِشَيْخٍ مِنْ أَهْلِ نَجْدٍ:
فَاسْتَقْدِرِ اللهَ خَيْرًا وَارْضَيَنَّ بِهِ * فَبَيْنَمَا الْعُسْرُ إِذْ دَارَتْ مَيَاسِيرُ
وَبَيْنَمَا الْمَرْءُ فِي الْأَحْيَاءِ مُغْتَبِطٌ * إِذْ صَارَ فِي الرَّمْسِ تَعْفُوهُ الْأَعَاصِيرُ
يَبْكِي عَلَيْهِ غَرِيبٌ لَيْسَ يَعْرِفُهُ * وَذُو قَرَابَتِهِ فِي الْحَيِّ مَسْرُورُ
حَتَّى كَأَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ إِلَّا تَذَكُّرُهُ * وَالدَّهْرُ أَيَّتَمَا حَالٍ دَهَارِيرُ
وَهٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ لِعُثْمَانَ بْنِ لَبِيدٍ الْعُذْرِيِّ.
paragraphs.en: Among what is related from Abū ʿAmr, by an old man of the people of Najd: Ask God to decree good for you and be content with it: while hardship is with you, easy times come round. While a man is among the living, envied for his lot, he is in the grave, and the whirlwinds efface it. A stranger who does not know him weeps for him, while his kinsman in the tribe is glad; until it is as if nothing were left of him but his remembrance; and time, in whatever state, brings misfortunes. These verses are by ʿUthmān ibn Labīd al-ʿUdhrī.

paragraphs.ar:
رَوَى هِشَامُ بْنُ الْكَلْبِيِّ قَالَ: عَاشَ عُبَيْدُ بْنُ شَرِيَّةَ الْجُرْهُمِيُّ ثَلَاثَمِائَةِ سَنَةٍ، وَأَدْرَكَ الْإِسْلَامَ فَأَسْلَمَ، وَدَخَلَ عَلَى مُعَاوِيَةَ بِالشَّامِ وَهُوَ خَلِيفَةٌ، فَقَالَ لَهُ: حَدِّثْنِي بِأَعْجَبِ مَا رَأَيْتَ. فَقَالَ: مَرَرْتُ ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ بِقَوْمٍ يَدْفِنُونَ مَيِّتًا لَهُمْ، فَلَمَّا انْتَهَيْتُ إِلَيْهِمُ اغْرَوْرَقَتْ عَيْنَايَ بِالدُّمُوعِ، وَتَمَثَّلْتُ بِقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ:
يَا قَلْبُ إِنَّكَ مِنْ أَسْمَاءَ مَغْرُورُ * فَاذْكُرْ وَهَلْ يَنْفَعَنْكَ الْيَوْمَ تَذْكِيرُ
قَدْ بُحْتَ بِالْحُبِّ مَا تُخْفِيهِ مُوجِدَةً * حَتَّى جَرَتْ لَكَ أَطْلَاقًا مَحَاضِيرُ
فَلَسْتَ تَدْرِي وَمَا تَدْرِي أَعَاجِلُهَا * أَدْنَى لِرُشْدِكَ أَمْ مَا فِيهِ تَأْخِيرُ
فَاسْتَقْدِرِ اللهَ خَيْرًا وَارْضَيَنَّ بِهِ * فَبَيْنَمَا الْعُسْرُ إِذْ دَارَتْ مَيَاسِيرُ
الْأَبْيَاتَ، إِلَى قَوْلِهِ:
يَبْكِي عَلَيْهِ غَرِيبٌ لَيْسَ يَعْرِفُهُ * وَذُو قَرَابَتِهِ فِي الْحَيِّ مَسْرُورُ
paragraphs.en: Hishām ibn al-Kalbī related: ʿUbayd ibn Sharya al-Jurhumī lived three hundred years. He lived into Islam and became a Muslim, and he went in to Muʿāwiya in Syria when he was caliph. Muʿāwiya said to him: Tell me the most wondrous thing you have seen. He said: One day I passed by some people who were burying one of their dead. When I came up to them my eyes filled with tears, and I quoted the words of the poet: O heart, you are deluded about Asmāʾ; remember — and will reminding do you any good today? You have disclosed in your passion the love that you were hiding, until swift steeds ran loose for you. You do not know, and cannot know, whether what comes soon is nearer to your good, or what is delayed. Ask God to decree good for you and be content with it: while hardship is with you, easy times come round — the verses, down to his words: A stranger who does not know him weeps for him, while his kinsman in the tribe is glad.

paragraphs.ar: قَالَ: فَقَالَ لِي رَجُلٌ: هَلْ تَعْرِفُ مَنْ قَالَ هٰذَا الشِّعْرَ؟ قُلْتُ: لَا. قَالَ: إِنَّ قَائِلَهُ هُوَ الَّذِي دَفَنَّاهُ السَّاعَةَ، وَأَنْتَ الْغَرِيبُ الَّذِي يَبْكِي عَلَيْهِ وَلَسْتَ تَعْرِفُهُ، وَهٰذَا الَّذِي خَرَجَ مِنْ قَبْرِهِ أَمَسُّ النَّاسِ رَحِمًا بِهِ، وَأَسَرُّهُمْ بِمَوْتِهِ. فَقَالَ لَهُ مُعَاوِيَةُ: لَقَدْ رَأَيْتَ عَجَبًا، فَمَنِ الْمَيِّتُ؟ فَقَالَ: عُثْمَانُ بْنُ لَبِيدٍ الْعُذْرِيُّ.
paragraphs.en: He said: A man said to me: Do you know who composed this poem? I said: No. He said: Its author is the man we have just buried. You are the stranger who weeps for him without knowing him, and this man coming away from his grave is his closest kinsman and the gladdest of men at his death. Muʿāwiya said to him: You have indeed seen a wonder. Who was the dead man? He said: ʿUthmān ibn Labīd al-ʿUdhrī.

paragraphs.ar:
وَحَكَى الْأَصْمَعِيُّ قَالَ: أَنْشَدَنَا أَبُو عَمْرٍو:
فَمَا جَبُنُوا أَنَّا نَشُدُّ عَلَيْهِمُ * وَلٰكِنْ رَأَوْا نَارًا تَحُشُّ وَتَسْفَعُ
قَالَ: فَذَكَرْتُ ذٰلِكَ لِشُعْبَةَ فَقَالَ: وَيْلَكَ، إِنَّمَا هِيَ تَحُسُّ وَتَسْفَعُ، أَيْ: تُحْرِقُ وَتُسَوِّدُ. قَالَ الْأَصْمَعِيُّ: قَدْ أَصَابَ أَبُو عَمْرٍو؛ لِأَنَّ مَعْنَى تَحُشُّ تُوقَدُ، وَقَدْ أَصَابَ شُعْبَةُ أَيْضًا، وَلَمْ أَرَ أَعْلَمَ بِالشِّعْرِ مِنْ شُعْبَةَ.
paragraphs.en: Al-Aṣmaʿī reported: Abū ʿAmr recited to us: They did not lose heart because we charged at them; rather they saw a fire that blazes (taḥushshu) and scorches. He said: I mentioned this to Shuʿba, and he said: Woe to you, it is only taḥussu wa-tasfaʿu, that is, it burns and blackens. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: Abū ʿAmr was right, because taḥushshu means it is kindled; and Shuʿba was right too. I have never seen anyone who knew poetry better than Shuʿba.

paragraphs.ar: وَرَوَى الْأَصْمَعِيُّ عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَلَاءِ قَالَ: سَمِعْتُ أَعْرَابِيًّا يَقُولُ: فُلَانٌ لَغُوبٌ، جَاءَتْهُ كِتَابِي فَاحْتَقَرَهَا. قَالَ: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ: أَتَقُولُ جَاءَتْهُ كِتَابِي؟ فَقَالَ: أَلَيْسَ بِصَحِيفَةٍ؟ فَحَمَلَهُ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى، وَقَدْ جَاءَ ذٰلِكَ كَثِيرًا فِي كَلَامِهِمْ. وَاللَّغُوبُ: الْأَحْمَقُ، وَلَهُ أَسْمَاءٌ كَثِيرَةٌ ذَكَرْنَاهَا مُسْتَوْفَاةً فِي كِتَابِنَا الْمَوْسُومِ بِالْفَائِقِ فِي أَسْمَاءِ الْمَائِقِ.
paragraphs.en: Al-Aṣmaʿī related that Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: I heard a Bedouin say: So-and-so is a lughūb; my letter (kitābī) came to him (jāʾathu, feminine) and he despised it (iḥtaqarahā). I said to him: Do you say jāʾathu kitābī? He said: Is it not a ṣaḥīfa (a sheet, feminine)? So he construed it by the sense, and this occurs often in their speech. A lughūb is a fool; the fool has many names, which we have given in full in our book entitled al-Fāʾiq fī asmāʾ al-māʾiq (The Excellent Book on the Names of the Fool).

paragraphs.ar: وَتُوُفِّيَ أَبُو عَمْرِو بْنُ الْعَلَاءِ فِي سَنَةِ أَرْبَعٍ وَخَمْسِينَ وَمِائَةٍ فِي خِلَافَةِ الْمَنْصُورِ.
paragraphs.en: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ died in the year one hundred and fifty-four, during the caliphate of al-Manṣūr.

entries.heading: أَبُو مُعَاوِيَةَ شَيْبَانُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمٰنِ التَّمِيمِيُّ النَّحْوِيُّ
entries.name: Abū Muʿāwiya Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Tamīmī al-Naḥwī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا أَبُو مُعَاوِيَةَ شَيْبَانُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمٰنِ التَّمِيمِيُّ النَّحْوِيُّ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ مَوْلًى لِبَنِي تَمِيمٍ، وَكَانَ يُعَلِّمُ أَوْلَادَ دَاوُدَ بْنِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللهِ بْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَكَانَ قَارِئًا مُحَدِّثًا نَحْوِيًّا مِنْ مُتَقَدِّمِي النَّحْوِيِّينَ، سَكَنَ الْكُوفَةَ زَمَانًا، وَانْتَقَلَ عَنْهَا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ، حَدَّثَ عَنِ الْحَسَنِ الْبَصْرِيِّ وَيَحْيَى بْنِ أَبِي كَثِيرٍ، وَحَدَّثَ عَنْهُ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمٰنِ بْنُ مَهْدِيٍّ وَغَيْرُهُ.
paragraphs.en: As for Abū Muʿāwiya Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Tamīmī al-Naḥwī, he was a client of the Banū Tamīm, and he taught the children of Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās. He was a Qurʾān reader, a transmitter of ḥadīth and a grammarian, one of the early grammarians. He lived in Kufa for a time and moved from there to Baghdad. He transmitted ḥadīth from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī and others transmitted from him.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ أَبُو أَحْمَدَ الْحَسَنُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللهِ بْنِ سَعِيدٍ الْعَسْكَرِيُّ: إِنَّ شَيْبَانَ النَّحْوِيَّ نِسْبَةٌ إِلَى بَطْنٍ يُقَالُ لَهُمْ نَحْوُ بْنُ شُمْسٍ، بِضَمِّ الشِّينِ، مِنْ بَطْنٍ مِنَ الْأَزْدِ. وَذَكَرَ أَبُو الْحُسَيْنِ بْنُ الْمُنَادِي أَنَّ الْمَنْسُوبَ إِلَى الْقَبِيلَةِ هُوَ يَزِيدُ النَّحْوِيُّ لَا شَيْبَانُ. قَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ بْنِ الْأَشْعَثِ: يَزِيدُ النَّحْوِيُّ هُوَ يَزِيدُ بْنُ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ، وَهُوَ مِنْ بَطْنٍ مِنَ الْأَزْدِ يُقَالُ لَهُمْ بَنُو نَحْوٍ، لَيْسَ مِنْ نَحْوِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ، وَلَمْ يَرْوِ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمُ الْحَدِيثَ إِلَّا رَجُلَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا يَزِيدُ هٰذَا، وَسَائِرُ مَنْ يُقَالُ لَهُ النَّحْوِيُّ فَمِنْ نَحْوِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ: شَيْبَانُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمٰنِ النَّحْوِيُّ، وَهَارُونُ بْنُ مُوسَى النَّحْوِيُّ، وَأَبُو زَيْدٍ.
paragraphs.en: Abū Aḥmad al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-ʿAskarī said: Shaybān al-Naḥwī's name refers to a clan called Naḥw ibn Shums (with u after the sh), a branch of al-Azd. Abū al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Munādī mentioned that the one named after that tribe is Yazīd al-Naḥwī, not Shaybān. Abū Bakr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sulaymān ibn al-Ashʿath said: Yazīd al-Naḥwī is Yazīd ibn Abī Saʿīd; he is of a branch of al-Azd called the Banū Naḥw, and not from naḥw, the grammar of Arabic. None of them transmitted ḥadīth except two men, one of whom is this Yazīd. All the others who are called al-Naḥwī are so called from naḥw, the grammar of Arabic: Shaybān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Naḥwī, Hārūn ibn Mūsā al-Naḥwī, and Abū Zayd.

paragraphs.ar: وَسُئِلَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ عَنْ شَيْبَانَ النَّحْوِيِّ، وَعَنْ هِشَامٍ الدَّسْتُوَائِيِّ، وَعَنْ حَرْبِ بْنِ شَدَّادٍ، فَقَالَ: شَيْبَانُ أَرْفَعُ عِنْدِي، شَيْبَانُ صَاحِبُ كِتَابٍ صَحِيحٍ، قَدْ رَوَى شَيْبَانُ عَنِ النَّاسِ، فَحَدِيثُهُ صَحِيحٌ. وَسُئِلَ يَحْيَى بْنُ مَعِينٍ عَنْ شَيْبَانَ: مَا حَالُهُ وَالْأَعْمَشُ؟ فَقَالَ: ثِقَةٌ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وَكَانَ يَحْيَى بْنُ مَعِينٍ يُوَثِّقُهُ، وَزَعَمَ أَنَّهُ بَصْرِيٌّ انْتَقَلَ إِلَى الْكُوفَةِ. وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَمَّارٍ: أَبُو مُعَاوِيَةَ النَّحْوِيُّ هُوَ بَصْرِيٌّ ثِقَةٌ.
paragraphs.en: The imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal was asked about Shaybān al-Naḥwī, Hishām al-Dastuwāʾī and Ḥarb ibn Shaddād, and he said: Shaybān ranks highest with me. Shaybān had a sound written collection; Shaybān transmitted from many people, and his ḥadīth is sound. Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn was asked about Shaybān: How does he stand with regard to al-Aʿmash? He said: Trustworthy in everything. Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn held him trustworthy, and he claimed that he was a Basran who had moved to Kufa. Ibn ʿAmmār said: Abū Muʿāwiya al-Naḥwī is a trustworthy Basran.

paragraphs.ar: وَتُوُفِّيَ بِبَغْدَادَ سَنَةَ أَرْبَعٍ وَسِتِّينَ وَمِائَةٍ فِي خِلَافَةِ الْمَهْدِيِّ، وَدُفِنَ فِي مَقْبَرَةِ الْخَيْزُرَانِ. وَقَالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سَعْدٍ: دُفِنَ فِي مَقَابِرِ قُرَيْشٍ بِبَابِ التِّبْنِ. وَقِيلَ: تُوُفِّيَ سَنَةَ سَبْعِينَ وَمِائَةٍ فِي خِلَافَةِ الْهَادِي.
paragraphs.en: He died in Baghdad in the year one hundred and sixty-four, during the caliphate of al-Mahdī, and was buried in the cemetery of al-Khayzurān. Muḥammad ibn Saʿd said: He was buried in the cemeteries of Quraysh at the Bāb al-Tibn. It is also said that he died in the year one hundred and seventy, during the caliphate of al-Hādī.

entries.heading: أَبُو عَبْدِ اللهِ هَارُونُ بْنُ مُوسَى
entries.name: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Hārūn ibn Mūsā al-Aʿwar

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا أَبُو عَبْدِ اللهِ هَارُونُ بْنُ مُوسَى، وَقِيلَ: أَبُو مُوسَى، الْقَارِئُ النَّحْوِيُّ الْأَعْوَرُ، فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبَصْرَةِ، وَكَانَ عَالِمًا بِالنَّحْوِ، وَسَمِعَ الْحَدِيثَ عَنْ طَاوُسٍ الْيَمَانِيِّ، وَثَابِتٍ الْبُنَانِيِّ، وَحُمَيْدٍ الطَّوِيلِ، وَرَوَى عَنْهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ الْجَعْدِ وَغَيْرُهُ.
paragraphs.en: As for Abū ʿAbd Allāh Hārūn ibn Mūsā — or, as some say, Abū Mūsā — the Qurʾān reader and grammarian, al-Aʿwar (the One-eyed), he was one of the people of Basra and was learned in grammar. He heard ḥadīth from Ṭāwūs al-Yamānī, Thābit al-Bunānī and Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, and ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd and others transmitted from him.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ بْنِ الْأَشْعَثِ: سَمِعْتُ أَبِي يَقُولُ: كَانَ هَارُونُ الْأَعْوَرُ يَهُودِيًّا فَأَسْلَمَ وَحَسُنَ إِسْلَامُهُ، وَحَفِظَ الْقُرْآنَ وَضَبَطَهُ، وَضَبَطَ النَّحْوَ، وَنَاظَرَهُ إِنْسَانٌ يَوْمًا فِي مَسْأَلَةٍ فَغَلَبَهُ هَارُونُ، فَلَمْ يَدْرِ الْمَغْلُوبُ مَا يَقُولُ، فَقَالَ لَهُ: أَنْتَ كُنْتَ يَهُودِيًّا وَأَسْلَمْتَ! فَقَالَ لَهُ هَارُونُ: بِئْسَ مَا صَنَعْتُ؟ قَالَ: فَغَلَبَهُ فِي هٰذَا أَيْضًا.
paragraphs.en: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sulaymān ibn al-Ashʿath said: I heard my father say: Hārūn al-Aʿwar was a Jew; he became a Muslim and was a good Muslim. He learned the Qurʾān by heart and mastered it, and he mastered grammar. One day a man disputed with him on a question and Hārūn got the better of him. The loser did not know what to say, and said to him: You were a Jew and became a Muslim! Hārūn said to him: Did I do wrong, then? And he got the better of him in this too.

paragraphs.ar: وَقَالَ أَبُو حَاتِمٍ السِّجِسْتَانِيُّ: سَأَلْتُ الْأَصْمَعِيَّ عَنْ هَارُونَ بْنِ مُوسَى النَّحْوِيِّ، فَقَالَ: كَانَ ثِقَةً مَأْمُونًا.
paragraphs.en: Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī said: I asked al-Aṣmaʿī about Hārūn ibn Mūsā al-Naḥwī, and he said: He was trustworthy and reliable.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “أبو عبد الله هارون بن موسى”. died: not in the entry; usually put at about 170/786.

entries.heading: شَرْقِيُّ بْنُ الْقُطَامِيِّ
entries.name: Sharqī ibn al-Quṭāmī

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا شَرْقِيُّ بْنُ الْقُطَامِيِّ فَكَانَ وَافِرَ الْأَدَبِ، عَالِمًا بِالنَّسَبِ، أَقْدَمَهُ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ الْمَنْصُورُ لِيُعَلِّمَ وَلَدَهُ الْمَهْدِيَّ الْأَدَبَ. وَشَرْقِيٌّ لَقَبٌ لَهُ، وَاسْمُهُ الْوَلِيدُ، وَالْقُطَامِيُّ لَقَبٌ لِوَالِدِهِ، وَاسْمُهُ الْحُصَيْنُ بْنُ جَمَالٍ، شَاعِرٌ كَلْبِيٌّ.
paragraphs.en: As for Sharqī ibn al-Quṭāmī, he had abundant learning in letters and knew the genealogies. Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr brought him to court to teach letters to his son al-Mahdī. Sharqī was his nickname; his name was al-Walīd. Al-Quṭāmī was his father's nickname; his name was al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Jamāl, a poet of Kalb.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُحْكَى عَنْ شَرْقِيِّ بْنِ الْقُطَامِيِّ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: دَخَلْتُ عَلَى الْمَنْصُورِ فَقَالَ: يَا شَرْقِيُّ، عَلَامَ يُؤْتَى الْمَرْءُ؟ فَقُلْتُ: أَصْلَحَ اللهُ تَعَالَى الْخَلِيفَةَ، عَلَى مَعْرُوفٍ قَدْ سَلَفَ، أَوْ مِثْلِهِ مُؤْتَنَفٍ، أَوْ قَدِيمِ شَرَفٍ، أَوْ عِلْمٍ مُطْرَفٍ.
paragraphs.en: It is reported that Sharqī ibn al-Quṭāmī said: I went in to al-Manṣūr, and he said: Sharqī, for what is a man favoured? I said: May God, exalted is He, keep the caliph in good health: for a kindness he has done in the past, or a like one newly done, or an ancient nobility, or a learning newly gained.

paragraphs.ar: قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْحَرْبِيُّ: شَرْقِيُّ بْنُ الْقُطَامِيِّ كُوفِيٌّ قَدْ تُكُلِّمَ فِيهِ، وَكَانَ صَاحِبَ سَمَرٍ. وَقَالَ زَكَرِيَّا بْنُ يَحْيَى السَّاجِيُّ: شَرْقِيُّ بْنُ الْقُطَامِيِّ ضَعِيفٌ، حَدَّثَ عَنْهُ شُعْبَةُ حَدِيثًا وَاحِدًا، وَلَيْسَ بِقَائِمٍ.
paragraphs.en: Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī said: Sharqī ibn al-Quṭāmī was a Kufan who has been criticised; he was a teller of night-time tales. Zakariyyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Sājī said: Sharqī ibn al-Quṭāmī is weak. Shuʿba transmitted one ḥadīth from him, and it is not sound.

entries.notes: Marginal heading: “شرقي بن القطامي”. died: not in the entry; usually put at about 150/767.

entries.heading: حَمَّادٌ الرَّاوِيَةُ
entries.name: Ḥammād al-Rāwiya

paragraphs.ar: وَأَمَّا حَمَّادٌ الرَّاوِيَةُ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكُوفَةِ، مَشْهُورًا بِرِوَايَةِ الْأَشْعَارِ وَالْأَخْبَارِ، وَهُوَ الَّذِي جَمَعَ السَّبْعَ الطِّوَالَ، هٰكَذَا ذَكَرَهُ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ النَّحَّاسُ، وَلَمْ يَثْبُتْ مَا ذَكَرَهُ النَّاسُ مِنْ أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ مُعَلَّقَةً عَلَى الْكَعْبَةِ.
paragraphs.en: As for Ḥammād al-Rāwiya (the Transmitter), he was one of the people of Kufa, famous for transmitting poems and reports. It was he who collected the Seven Long Poems; so Abū Jaʿfar Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Naḥḥās states. What people say, that they were hung up on the Kaʿba, is not established.

paragraphs.ar: وَيُحْكَى أَنَّ حَمَّادًا الرَّاوِيَةَ قَالَ: كُنْتُ مُنْقَطِعًا إِلَى يَزِيدَ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ، وَكَانَ أَخُوهُ هِشَامٌ يَجْفُونِي لِذٰلِكَ دُونَ سَائِرِ أَهْلِهِ مِنْ بَنِي أُمَيَّةَ فِي أَيَّامِ يَزِيدَ، فَلَمَّا مَاتَ يَزِيدُ وَأَفْضَتِ الْخِلَافَةُ إِلَى هِشَامٍ خِفْتُهُ، فَمَكَثْتُ فِي بَيْتِي سَنَةً لَا أَخْرُجُ إِلَّا لِمَنْ أَثِقُ بِهِ مِنْ إِخْوَانِي سِرًّا، فَلَمَّا لَمْ أَسْمَعْ أَحَدًا يَذْكُرُنِي أَمِنْتُ، فَخَرَجْتُ وَصَلَّيْتُ الْجُمُعَةَ فِي الرُّصَافَةِ، ثُمَّ جَلَسْتُ عِنْدَ بَابِ الْفِيلِ، فَإِذَا شُرْطِيَّانِ قَدْ وَقَفَا عَلَيَّ فَقَالَا: يَا حَمَّادُ، أَجِبِ الْأَمِيرَ يُوسُفَ بْنَ عُمَرَ. فَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي: هٰذَا الَّذِي كُنْتُ أَخَافُهُ. ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لَهُمَا: هَلْ لَكُمَا أَنْ تَدَعَانِي حَتَّى آتِيَ أَهْلِي فَأُوَدِّعَهُمْ وَدَاعَ مَنْ لَا يَرْجِعُ إِلَيْهِمْ أَبَدًا، ثُمَّ أَصِيرَ مَعَكُمَا؟ فَقَالَا: مَا إِلَى ذٰلِكَ سَبِيلٌ. فَاسْتَسْلَمْتُ فِي أَيْدِيهِمَا، وَصِرْتُ إِلَى يُوسُفَ بْنِ عُمَرَ وَهُوَ فِي الْإِيوَانِ الْأَحْمَرِ، فَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيَّ السَّلَامَ، وَرَمَى إِلَيَّ كِتَابًا فِيهِ: بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ، مِنْ عَبْدِ اللهِ هِشَامٍ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ إِلَى يُوسُفَ بْنِ عُمَرَ، أَمَّا بَعْدُ، فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ كِتَابِي هٰذَا فَابْعَثْ إِلَى حَمَّادٍ الرَّاوِيَةِ مَنْ يَأْتِيكَ بِهِ غَيْرَ مُرَوَّعٍ وَلَا مُتَعْتَعٍ، وَادْفَعْ إِلَيْهِ خَمْسَمِائَةِ دِينَارٍ وَجَمَلًا مَهْرِيًّا يَسِيرُ عَلَيْهِ اثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ لَيْلَةً إِلَى دِمَشْقَ. فَأَخَذْتُ الدَّنَانِيرَ، وَنَظَرْتُ فَإِذَا جَمَلٌ مَرْحُولٌ، فَجَعَلْتُ رِجْلِي فِي الْغَرْزِ، وَسِرْتُ اثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ لَيْلَةً حَتَّى وَافَيْتُ دِمَشْقَ.
paragraphs.en: It is reported that Ḥammād al-Rāwiya said: I was attached to Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and for that reason his brother Hishām treated me coldly, unlike the rest of his family of the Banū Umayya, in the days of Yazīd. When Yazīd died and the caliphate passed to Hishām, I feared him, and I stayed in my house for a year, going out only in secret to those of my friends whom I trusted. When I heard no one mention me, I felt safe; I went out, prayed the Friday prayer in al-Ruṣāfa, and then sat by the Elephant Gate. Suddenly two policemen stood over me and said: Ḥammād, answer the summons of the governor Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar. I said to myself: This is what I feared. Then I said to them: Will you let me go to my family and bid them farewell, as one who will never return to them, and then come with you? They said: That cannot be. So I gave myself up into their hands and was brought to Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar, who was in the Red Hall. I greeted him and he returned my greeting, and he tossed me a letter, in which was written: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. From the servant of God Hishām, Commander of the Faithful, to Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar. To proceed: when you read this letter of mine, send someone to Ḥammād al-Rāwiya to bring him to you without alarming or harassing him, and give him five hundred dinars and a Mahrī camel on which he may travel twelve nights to Damascus. I took the dinars, and looked, and there was a saddled camel. I put my foot in the stirrup and travelled for twelve nights until I reached Damascus.

paragraphs.ar: وَنَزَلْتُ عَلَى بَابِ هِشَامٍ، فَاسْتَأْذَنْتُ فَأُذِنَ لِي، فَدَخَلْتُ عَلَيْهِ فِي دَارٍ قَوْرَاءَ مَفْرُوشَةٍ بِالرُّخَامِ، وَهُوَ فِي مَجْلِسٍ مَفْرُوشٍ بِالرُّخَامِ، وَبَيْنَ كُلِّ رُخَامَتَيْنِ قَضِيبٌ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ، وَحِيطَانُهُ كَذٰلِكَ، وَهِشَامٌ جَالِسٌ عَلَى طِنْفِسَةٍ حَمْرَاءَ، وَعَلَيْهِ ثِيَابٌ حُمْرٌ مِنَ الْخَزِّ، وَقَدْ تَضَمَّخَ بِالْمِسْكِ وَالْعَنْبَرِ، وَبَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِسْكٌ مَفْتُوتٌ فِي أَوَانِي ذَهَبٍ يُقَلِّبُهُ بِيَدِهِ فَتَفُوحُ رَوَائِحُهُ، فَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيَّ السَّلَامَ، وَاسْتَدْنَانِي فَدَنَوْتُ حَتَّى قَبَّلْتُ رِجْلَهُ، فَإِذَا جَارِيَتَانِ لَمْ أَرَ مِثْلَهُمَا قَطُّ، فِي أُذُنَيْ كُلِّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُمَا حَلْقَتَانِ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ فِيهِمَا لُؤْلُؤَتَانِ تَتَوَقَّدَانِ.
paragraphs.en: I alighted at Hishām's gate and asked leave to enter. It was granted, and I went in to him in a spacious house paved with marble. He was in a hall paved with marble, with a rod of gold between every two slabs, and its walls were the same. Hishām was sitting on a red cushion, wearing red clothes of silk, perfumed with musk and ambergris, and before him was crumbled musk in vessels of gold, which he turned over with his hand so that its scent spread. I greeted him and he returned my greeting, and he bade me come near. I came near and kissed his foot. There were two slave-girls the like of whom I had never seen, in the ears of each of them two rings of gold, in which two pearls glowed.

paragraphs.ar:
فَقَالَ لِي: كَيْفَ أَنْتَ يَا حَمَّادُ، وَكَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟ فَقُلْتُ: بِخَيْرٍ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ. قَالَ: أَتَدْرِي فِيمَا بَعَثْتُ إِلَيْكَ؟ قُلْتُ: لَا. قَالَ: بَعَثْتُ إِلَيْكَ لِبَيْتٍ خَطَرَ بِبَالِي لَمْ أَدْرِ مَنْ قَائِلُهُ. قُلْتُ: مَا هُوَ؟ قَالَ:
وَدَعَوْا بِالصَّبُوحِ يَوْمًا فَجَاءَتْ * قَيْنَةٌ فِي يَمِينِهَا إِبْرِيقُ
فَقُلْتُ: يَقُولُهُ عَدِيُّ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِي قَصِيدَةٍ لَهُ. قَالَ: أَنْشِدْنِيهَا. فَأَنْشَدْتُهُ:
بَكَرَ الْعَاذِلُونَ فِي وَضَحِ الصُّبْ * حِ يَقُولُونَ لِي أَلَا تَسْتَفِيقُ
وَيَلُومُونَ فِيكِ يَا ابْنَةَ عَبْدِ الْ * لَّهِ وَالْقَلْبُ عِنْدَكُمْ مَوْثُوقُ
لَسْتُ أَدْرِي إِذْ أَكْثَرُوا الْعَذْلَ فِيهَا * أَعَدُوٌّ يَلُومُنِي أَمْ صَدِيقُ
قَالَ: إِلَى أَنِ انْتَهَيْتُ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ:
وَدَعَوْا بِالصَّبُوحِ يَوْمًا فَجَاءَتْ * قَيْنَةٌ فِي يَمِينِهَا إِبْرِيقُ
قَدَّمَتْهُ عَلَى عُقَارٍ كَعَيْنِ الدْ * دِيكِ صَفَّى سُلَافَهَا الرَّاوُوقُ
مُرَّةٍ قَبْلَ مَزْجِهَا فَإِذَا مَا * مُزِجَتْ لَذَّ طَعْمُهَا مَنْ يَذُوقُ
وَطَفَا فَوْقَهَا فَقَاقِيعُ كَالْيَا * قُوتِ حُمْرٌ يَزِينُهَا التَّصْفِيقُ
ثُمَّ كَانَ الْمِزَاجُ مَاءَ سَحَابٍ * لَا صَرًى آجِنٌ وَلَا مَطْرُوقُ
paragraphs.en: He said to me: How are you, Ḥammād, and how do you fare? I said: Well, Commander of the Faithful. He said: Do you know why I sent for you? I said: No. He said: I sent for you because of a verse that came to my mind, and I did not know who composed it. I said: What is it? He said: “And one day they called for the morning draught, and a singing-girl came with a ewer in her right hand.” I said: ʿAdī ibn Zayd says it, in a poem of his. He said: Recite it to me. So I recited to him: The reproachers came early, in the first light of morning, saying to me: Will you not come to your senses? They blame me for you, daughter of ʿAbd Allāh, while my heart is bound fast with you. I do not know, when they reproach me so much about her, whether it is an enemy who blames me or a friend. He said: Until I came to his words: And one day they called for the morning draught, and a singing-girl came with a ewer in her right hand. She brought it forward with wine like a cock's eye, whose first running the strainer had cleared: bitter before it is mixed, but when it is mixed, its taste is sweet to whoever tastes it. Above it float bubbles like red rubies, made lovely by the pouring. Then the mixing water was rain from the clouds, neither brackish and stale nor fouled.

paragraphs.ar: قَالَ: فَطَرِبَ، وَقَالَ لِي: أَحْسَنْتَ وَاللهِ يَا حَمَّادُ، يَا جَارِيَةُ اسْقِيهِ. فَسَقَتْنِي شَرْبَةً ذَهَبَتْ بِثُلُثِ عَقْلِي، فَقَالَ: أَعِدْ. فَأَعَدْتُ، فَاسْتَخَفَّهُ الطَّرَبُ حَتَّى نَزَلَ عَنْ فُرُشِهِ، ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْجَارِيَةِ الْأُخْرَى: اسْقِيهِ. فَسَقَتْنِي، فَذَهَبَ ثُلُثٌ آخَرُ مِنْ عَقْلِي، ثُمَّ قَالَ: سَلْ حَاجَتَكَ. فَقُلْتُ: كَائِنَةً مَا كَانَتْ؟ قَالَ: نَعَمْ. قُلْتُ: إِحْدَى هَاتَيْنِ الْجَارِيَتَيْنِ. قَالَ: هُمَا جَمِيعًا لَكَ بِمَا عَلَيْهِمَا وَمَا لَهُمَا. ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْأُولَى: اسْقِيهِ. فَسَقَتْنِي شَرْبَةً سَقَطْتُ مِنْهَا، فَلَمْ أَعْقِلْ حَتَّى أَصْبَحْتُ وَالْجَارِيَتَانِ عِنْدَ رَأْسِي، وَإِذَا عَشَرَةٌ مِنَ الْخَدَمِ مَعَ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ بَدْرَةٌ، فَقَالَ أَحَدُهُمْ: إِنَّ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَقْرَأُ عَلَيْكَ السَّلَامَ، وَيَقُولُ لَكَ: خُذْ هٰذِهِ فَانْتَفِعْ بِهَا فِي سَفَرِكَ. فَأَخَذْتُهَا وَالْجَارِيَتَيْنِ، وَعَاوَدْتُ أَهْلِي. وَاللهُ أَعْلَمُ.
paragraphs.en: He said: He was moved with delight, and said to me: Well done, by God, Ḥammād! Girl, give him to drink. She gave me a draught that took away a third of my wits. He said: Recite it again. I recited it again, and delight so carried him away that he came down from his cushions. Then he said to the other girl: Give him to drink. She gave me to drink, and another third of my wits went. Then he said: Ask for what you want. I said: Whatever it may be? He said: Yes. I said: One of these two slave-girls. He said: They are both yours, with all they wear and all they own. Then he said to the first: Give him to drink. She gave me a draught from which I fell down, and I knew nothing until morning, when the two girls were at my head, and there were ten servants, each with a purse of money. One of them said: The Commander of the Faithful greets you and says to you: Take this and make use of it on your journey. I took it and the two girls, and went back to my family. And God knows best.
